DECISION OP PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement with respect to interprovincial and international highway transport.
In view of the decision of the privy council in the case of Winner v. S.M.T. (Eastern) Limited et al., it appears that an interprovincial or international undertaking within the meaning of section 92, head 10(a) of the British North America Act, is not subject to the provincial law relating to public carriers.
In our view it would not be in the public interest to have a divided jurisdiction, with the provincial boards controlling the traffic within the provinces, and a federal board controlling the traffic moving between the provinces or between a province and the United States, and for this amongst other reasons we are reluctant to enter this field and thereby bring about divided jurisdiction.
In view of this situation I propose to call a conference of provincial ministers having jurisdiction over highways to discuss the problems arising herein and to endeavour to find a common ground on the best way to regulate and control highway transport, whether intraprovincial, interprovincial or international.
Among ten provinces, all interested in the control of the traffic using their highways, there may be different views expressed on this subject. I am hopeful that a common understanding may be reached to the end that the provinces will be able to regulate and control all motor transport using provincial highways.

subtopic: DECISION OP PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question. I take it that it is the hope of the government that the board of transport commissioners will not be called upon to exercise any jurisdiction over highways, and that no other dominion government body will be called upon to exercise such jurisdiction either.

speechtext:
This afternoon I would like to bring the history of the discussion on unemployment up a little closer to our own time and quote from some of the proceedings in this house relating to the year 1935. At that time our representatives here in parliament were having a debate on unemployment and the leader of the opposition of that day, Mr. William Lyon Mackenzie King, was speaking on the state of affairs in Canada as the result of five years of Conservative administration. He told us in this speech, as reported at page 59 of Hansard of 1935, that there were at that time over one million people on direct relief. He added that the total was not as great as it had been two years previously when 1,240,000 were unemployed, but that there were still over one million on relief, which was being paid from dominion, provincial and the other sources concerned.
I should like to remind hon. members that this was stated in the house after five years of Conservative administration, after five years in office by a government which had come into office on the promise that it would cure this problem of unemployment. But before our Liberal friends become too excited we will move on to 1936, when they were back in office again. In this connection I should like to quote from a speech delivered by my friend Mr. C. G. MacNeil, at that time the member for Vancouver North. He said then that in December last there were in Canada 1,206,429 persons in receipt of some form of relief. In February, 1935, there were 1,054,821, and in February, 1934, there were 1,154,822 persons receiving some form of relief. He suggested at that time that this number included some 400,000 wholly unemployed wage earners.
The point I wish to stress is this. I have no wish to throw stones at past administrations. I realize that those who were in charge of the government at that time were facing a situation which had no precedent in human history and that they grappled with it presumably to the best of their ability. In fact, it is to their credit, Mr. Speaker, that they apparently took the symptoms and signs of economic decay much more seriously than their counterpart of the present day.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we must remember that at that time we did not have in the seats of office the intellectual giants we have today. But even such minor political figures as the late Mr. Mackenzie King, the late Viscount Bennett and their colleagues-and they had a certain measure of political standing were unable to do anything about this problem, although at least they admitted that there was a problem. Today we have government spokesmen-and the leading one among them is the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe)- refusing to admit that there is any serious situation at all in the country.
Last night I quoted some figures from Messrs. Dun and Bradstreet. This afternoon I should like to quote some figures from the dominion bureau of statistics. In fact, I would recommend these to the Acting Prime Minister as desirable reading at the present time. Here we have a table of commercial failures in Canada, showing the assets and liabilities for the third quarter of 1953, with comparisons with the third quarters of other years. These are extremely interesting figures because, by the comparisons they draw, they show us precisely what is happening in our economy. They go back as far as the year 1929. In the third quarter of that year the total liabilities of commercial failures had been $9,300,000. Then we move up to 1932, when we find that the situation had improved a little bit and that we had only $8,791,000. Then in 1939 when, of course, we were beginning to get into the war, when by the help of war expenditures we were rapidly coming out of the depression, we had failures amounting to only $3,789,000. Five years later, in 1944, just towards the end of the war, we had a mere three-quarters of a million dollars of liabilities in our commercial failures. But from that date on the figures got steadily worse. In 1947 the liabilities were $2,500,000; in 1948, they were $4,139,000; in 1950, $5,798,000; in 1951, $6,469,000; in 1952, $6,750,000; and in the third quarter of 1953, last year, $8,074,000.
I think we have here, without any doubt, plain evidence in front of us that there is something radically wrong with our economy, something that will not be cured by mere glad cries of optimism, and something that I think should be studied by all responsible people today, particularly those who are in the seats of office.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
Oh yes; you people
opposite do well to pound your desks because, Mr. Speaker, there were a lot of mediocrities, nonentities and plain political knotheads who came into power on the coattails of the extremely able Acting Prime Minister. I am very much afraid that when he goes the way of all flesh, some of them will also go the way of all flesh. However, as I say, this optimistic spirit coming from a man of the capacity of the Acting Prime Minister gives one pause. If he were a stupid or an ignorant man or if he were a man with no experience, we could dismiss his statements with a shrug of the shoulders. But when we know what kind of man he is; when we know the job he did during the war when, as a result in no small measure of his vigour and his activities, and his ability to organize, we came out of the depression as revealed by the figures I have just quoted, I think we have the right to expect that now, when we are facing another serious problem, the right hon. gentleman will consent to apply his mind to that problem and to seek a solution for it rather than seek to persuade us that no problem exists. In fact, Mr. Speaker, when I hear the right hon. gentleman giving voice to these optimistic predictions, I am reminded of a famous gentleman of some years ago-some hon. members of my age will remember him;
I refer to Dr. Coue-who was going to solve all our problems by the simple little formula of saying over and over again to himself and everybody around him, "Every day, in every way, things are getting better and better". Of course they did not get better. Dr. Coue flourished during the darkest days of the depression. Since then he has disappeared from view unless indeed, Mr. Speaker, we have now discovered what became of Dr. Coue, and find that he has become the Acting Prime Minister of Canada.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, when I see this man to whom Canada owes a most tremendous debt-and I hope he realizes I am saying this in all sincerity-I wonder why it is that we cannot call on him today to face this extremely serious problem that confronts us.
The other day when my colleague the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) was speaking, some comments were made from the right of us here with regard to the curtailment of wages or the fixing of wages.
I have here today some figures to show that


that perhaps is not the area in our economy that we should be worrying too much about and that perhaps we would be better advised to turn to some of the other areas in the economy. For instance, we might turn to the report presented to us by the superintendent of insurance for Canada, who gives us some very interesting information on page 7 of his preparatory index. He tells us that out of every $100 income of the life insurance companies, there was expended in disbursements under contracts, $36.88; for general expenses, $16.65; taxes, $1.52; other disbursements including dividends, $10.44, making a total of $65.49. There was left to be carried to reserves an amount of $35.51 out of every $100 collected.
As the superintendent of insurance also tells us, the total income of life insurance companies in Canada in the year 1951 was $839,500,000. We can assume that nearly $300 million was taken from the pockets of the Canadian people by the life insurance companies and placed in their reserves. I know, of course, that many people will say that these vast sums have to be invested in order to ensure the safety of the policyholders. I regret to say, however, that that is a complete delusion. Here we have to deal not with an ordinary type of business but really with what is after all merely a legalized form of gambling. Let us take one particular company which is reported at page 408 of the report of the superintendent of insurance. This particular company reports $19 J million for premium income and investment income of $5,500,000. It also reports that its disbursements in insurance and annuity contracts amounted to $8J million. The interesting point about this is that, in spite of all its investments, this company is obliged to rely on its continuing stream of premium income in order to fulfil its obligations to its policyholders. Having done that, and having paid all its other costs of $7,110,000, it had a surplus of some $12 million. This is the point that I have been coming to.
In connection with this question of unemployment we cannot overlook the government's policy with regard to the investment of the surplus savings of the Canadian people. Here is a large pool of these savings which we are permitting to fall into the hands of a comparatively small group of corporations and over which, as we have seen only too painfully in recent weeks, the government has little or no control. All its efforts to induce investment of these funds in the areas in which the government considers they should be invested appear to be falling on deaf ears.
The figures that I have quoted are .merely symptoms of the underlying disease of our

society which was plain to be seen in the 1930's and which was not cured by this government or its predecessors but was cured entirely by force of circumstances. It was cured because of the necessity of turning from our unplanned dog-eat-dog economy to a planned economy fixed on certain goals. I would point out that although it was popular to say throughout the debates from 1930 to 1935, as it is today, that the depressed condition of the world was the result of world-wide circumstances over which no government had any control, nevertheless the measures which were taken under the extremely capable and vigorous leadership of the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) were in final essence purely domestic measures completely within the competence of the government of Canada.
I would point out that, although vast quantities of materials were shipped abroad to Canada's allies, vast quantities of materials and machines of destruction were sent to our own forces in the field and large loans were made to our allies, in the final analysis the Canadian people paid for every cent of those expenditures and it was entirely the domestic measures that were taken which, incidental to helping to win the war, solved the economic problems of Canada of that day. These problems are now coming home again to us, and I think the Canadian people have the right to ask this government, which assumed power with such a fanfare of trumpets last August, what it proposes to do now in the present circumstances.
I must confess that I have been bitterly disappointed at the statements of government spokesmen in this regard, and particularly disappointed with statements of the Acting Prime Minister because, as I have said before, he is a man of outstanding capacity, vigour and attainments. The only conclusion I can come to is that perhaps the situation is like that of an old French woman I heard of once who, after peering out the window for six weeks at incessant rain, gave it as her considered opinion that ce bon Dieu was getting too old for His job. I wonder if we are perhaps in the same circumstances today and whether we have to have a complete change of administration before we can hope to have these problems tackled with the same vigour with which they were tackled in the 1930's.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to follow in any detail the arguments we have just heard from the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron). However, I should like to take exception to certain remarks he made at the beginning of his speech last night. The hon. member at
Proposed Committee on Unemployment that time was referring to the situation in 1929 and the fact that the government of the day had claimed that everything was very rosy and that there was then prosperity in the country. The hon. member for Nanaimo went on to say, as found at page 2343 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, one might almost have imagined that the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) was speaking. Yes; and then, as my Conservative friend says, "came the deluge". But the deluge was in the form of a Conservative government, which arrived in 1930.
We have heard that statement made in varying forms over a long period of years. I am not surprised when I hear it made by some people outside the house, perhaps in back country districts where they have not had much opportunity to study history, but I must say that I am very much surprised to hear it made by a member of parliament, one of our so-called $10,000 a year men. I should like to call his attention to the fact that the deluge also came in the United States, and it came under the Republican government of Mr. Hoover, who I suppose is one of the greatest men produced in the United States in the last thirty-five or forty years.
I should now like to call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that in Great Britain in 1929 none other than Ramsay MacDonald, the Labour leader, headed the government of that country, and the deluge to which the hon. member referred as coming about in Canada under a Conservative government happened to just as great an extent in Great Britain under Ramsay MacDonald, the Labour leader. I could go on and refer to France. I can come nearer home and refer to the situation that existed in Newfoundland, which at that time was not a part of Canada. We remember that the situation became so bad there that a commission of government was formed and the affairs of the country were conducted under a commission for quite a number of years.
These wisecracks, if I may call them that, and they are nothing more or less than cheap wisecracks to anyone who knows anything about the situation in Canada and other countries in the past twenty-five years, have no place today in arguments in the House of Commons. The fact of the matter is that from 1929 to 1940 almost no country in the world was in a position to repair its economic situation any better than we did in Canada.
I think it is about time that that sort of argument was relegated to the past.
I wish to say a few words about the unemployment situation in Canada today. We have had a very interesting debate, although it is perhaps unfortunate that a debate of
2354	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment this kind is necessary at the present time. There has been some disagreement as to the amount of unemployment in Canada. The labour leaders of the country claim that there are something like 530,000 out of work. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) states that the number is nearer 280,000 or 300,000. Be that as it may, I do not think this is the time to either exaggerate or minimize the situation in any way. I know something about conditions in my own province and the maritime provinces generally. Possibly I may be pardoned if I confine my remarks to that part of Canada particularly.
I should like to point out, because it is a known fact, that when a recession hits this country it always seems to strike the maritime provinces first and always seems to hit them the hardest. That there is in the mari-times a situation which is not good is not merely my opinion but that of some of the outstanding men in that part of the country. I should like to refer to the remarks made by Dr. Coady of St. Francis Xavier University when only a few weeks ago he was speaking to a convention of fishermen in the town of Amherst. He had this to say about conditions:
Our present recession in the maritime provinces, amounting almost to a depression, is embarrassing and saddening.
That was Dr. Coady's opinion. And I might point out-although perhaps it is not necessary-that Dr. Coady is one of the outstanding economists and students of economics in this country. He is also one of the most practical economists in the Dominion of Canada.
I would also like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Moncton Times a short time ago under the heading "Shocks to Economic Stability of New Brunswick." I am not going to quote the whole editorial. It speaks about the situation in general in our province, and concludes in this way:
These shocks to the economic stability of New Brunswick are definitely a cause for serious concern. Indeed, the situation which has developed to adversely affect a growing number of the workers in this province clearly calls for immediate and direct intervention by the federal administration to activate any of the work projects claimed to be in readiness to counteract the trends towards a recession at the outset.
I shall not quote any further articles or newspaper editorials. What are these shocks to the economic stability of the maritime provinces, and to New Brunswick in particular? Well, I might point out first of all the textile industry in our province. Mention has already been made of this industry. In the textile mill in the town of Marysville, very near the city of Fredericton, the home of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), 550


men have been let out of employment. But that is not the worst feature. The factory itself has been closed down, and closed down permanently. This is a factory which has been operating in that part of the country for three-quarters of a century or more. This does not mean only that the people employed in the mill are being laid off; it means that this industry, around which the town has been built and the whole life of the community developed, is now out of business. Not only are the men who worked in the factory affected, but also it has affected the merchants, the businessmen, the taxi men- all these people. And you must add to the 550 in the town of Marysville who are out of employment all these others who depend indirectly upon the factory for their work.
These people have been trained to do a definite kind of work. They cannot very easily go out and find employment in other jobs, because they are textile workers. Their fathers before them were textile workers. Their grandfathers were textile workers. Their children are textile workers. Through the generations all these people have been working in this industry, and when the industry is closed down it means far more than would appear on the surface.
Not only is the town of Marysville affected, but the town of Milltown and other large textile centres are suffering similar difficulties. I do not know whether the mill at Mill-town is going to close down or not, but I do know that in the last few months 690 employees have been laid off.
Another large lay-off we have had in the maritime provinces has been in our railways, and this affects more than the maritime provinces. I know my own province and the town of Moncton perhaps better than I know the rest of the area affected, and I can tell the house that 240 men have been laid off in the last few weeks. Moncton is the Canadian National Railways centre; and I am informed that at McAdam, the Canadian Pacific Railway centre, a similar number have been discharged from employment. I am told that in Moncton alone the loss of employment suffered by these 240 to whom I have referred means a loss in payroll amounting to $600,000 in that community. One can readily understand what that means to the economic life of a city of moderate size.
We might very well ask ourselves the reason for this decline in work on our railways. Well, I have my own opinion, and it is that at least one reason is the lack of freight being shipped overseas and entering from overseas. As we know, almost 60 per cent of our trade in recent years has been with the United States. This means that the

Proposed Committee on Unemployment
railway companies are not receiving the amount of freight they otherwise would have. Of necessity our freight is moving north and south instead of east and west. The economy of this country was built up for trade to move from the centre of the country to the Pacific and Atlantic ports. Our great ports of Vancouver, Montreal, Quebec, Halifax and Saint John were all built on an economy under which they would be fed by the east-west railways, and on the understanding that our trade would flow overseas.
In the last few years, owing perhaps to the fact that we could not get overseas trade, our trade has been flowing north and south more than it is east and west. The Moncton Times of January 30 had this to say about car loadings in Canada:
In the period from July 1 to December 31, 1953. revenue loadings were consistently below the comparable months of 1952, December recording a particularly marked drop of 13 per cent. It was the lowest figure to be registered in that month since 1949. Taking the entire year 1953 the total tonnage moved reached 119,343,000 tons, a drop of 6 million tons or 42 per cent from the 1952 total movement.
As I say, that is the reason that these men are out of work in Moncton and McAdam, and other railway centres across Canada.
The port of Saint John has found it a very dull winter. I heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) make reference yesterday to trade in the city of Vancouver. It appears that this year most of our wheat has been shipped through that port instead of through Atlantic ports. This is just one reason, of course; but it is one reason why the situation has been bad at Saint John and Halifax. Mr. J. G. Farquahar, special representative of the Canadian international trade fair, made a report a short time ago which appeared in a recent issue of the Loyalist, a paper published in Saint John. The article is headed:
Heavy business loss for port; cargo drops 464,000 tons.
It refers to the port of Saint John. The article goes on to say:
While 1953 showed an encouraging increase of some 50,000 tons in imports, and grain exports increased materially, the exportation of general cargo declined 464,000 tons, or about 35 per cent.
Then he makes reference to the discontinuance of the Marshall plan, which really does not have much to do with the subject, so far as the port of Saint John is concerned. But the fact of the matter is that the import and export of goods through the port of Saint John had declined to the extent of some 35 per cent which, as I am sure everyone will agree, is a very high percentage.
I could also speak about lumbering and pit props and the loss to these industries
in New Brunswick. I have spoken of it in the house before, and our party has spoken of it a number of times. We have pointed out that because of the lack of convertibility of sterling it has been almost impossible for us to sell our lumber and pit prop products in Great Britain. This also means a great loss in employment as far as our particular section of the country is concerned.
When he was speaking the other day, the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) mentioned the fishing industry, and I shall not deal with it this afternoon. The mining industry in the maritimes was dealt with fully by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). That is more or less the picture of the maritime provinces, and particularly of my own province of New Brunswick. I do not wish to paint too black a picture. I realize that there has been seasonal unemployment in our province and in our section nearly every year, but I do wish to point out that at the present time it has reached a stage that is not seasonal, and something must be done to correct the situation.
What happens when our people become unemployed? We have had unemployment during the very best times. We have had good times in Canada since the last war, but many of our people had to go to Ontario, to Quebec and to other parts of Canada to obtain employment. They have two alternatives: one is to migrate to some other part of the country and the other is to join the army.
Only last Sunday as I was walking up Elgin street I met a young man in uniform. I did not know him, but he knew me. He had been in my basic training centre in Fredericton during the war, he said. He came from Moncton. He was in uniform and on his way to Petawawa. I asked him when he joined up. He said: "I have lost my job with the Canadian National Railways in Moncton and I and four other boys are going through to Petawawa to join the army." He was a young married man, 35 years old, with two children. He told me that besides working on the railway he had spent three years before that as an apprentice with the railway. That man has had to give up practically his life's work. Now he has joined the army and gone to Petawawa. These are just natural results of the situation that I have outlined.
What does the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) say with reference to unemployment and the government's responsibility? Well, I shall quote one paragraph which is to be found at page 2089 of Hansard of February 15:
The provinces have responsibilities to help guard their people against hardship. I for one have no
2356	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment reason to believe other than that the provinces are effectively helping this winter if and where they find it necessary.
I agree that the provinces have some responsibilities. There is no question about that. But these instances of unemployment in the country that I have mentioned are all due to the policies of the federal government and not in any way due to any action of the provincial government. I contend that the full responsibility for the unemployment in the country at the present time is the federal government's. It is all very well to say that the provincial governments have responsibility. The people who are living in the provinces cannot get away, and the provinces must of necessity help in some way. So far as the basic responsibility is concerned, I contend it is entirely the federal government's.
Let us take Marysville, a mill town. So far as the provincial government is concerned, it has no responsibility there for what has happened. I know that the provincial government, probably in co-operation with the Minister of Labour, is doing all it can. It is trying to encourage some other industry to come to that town. I am afraid the provincial government will have a difficult time in that regard. I would say the Department of Defence Production has a responsibility there. I have said this time and time again. At Marysville we have a factory that employed some 550 men. We are putting out hundreds of millions of dollars for defence production in this country. If some private concern does not take over the operation of some industry in that town, here is an opportunity for the federal government to do some work there in connection with defence production. The town has the men; it has the mill; and the federal government owes it to our province.
The last issue of the defence production report that I read showed that out of millions spent in this country on defence production only $50,000 was spent in New Brunswick and nearly half of that went to the Swift Company of Moncton for meat which is brought in from other parts of Canada. This matter should be thoroughly investigated. There is a great responsibility on the federal government which they could and should assume. I am also satisfied that the local government can and will do all that is within its power.
I now come to the amendment of the opposition, and I should like to read the last paragraph:
Now, therefore, be it resolved that this house is of the opinion that a select committee should be appointed immediately for the purpose of examining into and reporting upon the actual unemployment situation throughout Canada and for the


purpose of making recommendations to this house as to short-term and long-term methods for dealing effectively with this problem.
I might point out that when he spoke the other day the minister said that we have unemployment insurance. We had unemployment insurance before this mass unemployment occurred. The minister also mentioned family allowances and old age pensions. We had family allowances and old age pensions when there was a hundred per cent employment in this country. As far as old age pensions are concerned, they have nothing to do with employment. They are paid only to people 70 years of age and over, people who are not in the unemployment ranks at all.
Let me take our amendment, which I consider is divided into three parts. First, it has to do with the unemployment situation and the number of unemployed in the country. As I said, there has been considerable doubt as to the number. The minister's department contends that it is around 300,000. The heads of the labour unions claim that it is over 500,000, and we have had figures even higher than that. A committee such as is recommended by our amendment would find out definitely what the unemployment situation is in this country. I think that is the first thing that should be found out. We want to get the facts. We do not want to see the situation exaggerated, and certainly by no means do we want to see it minimized.
The second recommendation in the amendment is that there should be some short-term method of looking after unemployment. That seems to me to be a recommendation that we more or less speed up certain public works programs in order to look after the situation at the present time. There are possibly men and women who are hungry today, a situation which should not be allowed to continue. The short-term method which is recommended would be something that could be put into force at once, so that in these times, when there is plenty in this country, there would be no one going hungry.
The third recommendation is that a longterm method be adopted. I think that this is the most important. We should do something in order to see that this condition does not recur to any great extent. There are a great many people in this country who think there should not be any unemployment at all. We are a great rich country; we have everything in abundance. If proper steps are taken there is no reason why there should not be employment for every man or woman who wants employment in this dominion of Canada.
We are considered, and rightly so, to be the most fortunate people in the world today. I would point out that Canada was not

devastated in any way during the last war. European countries and countries in other parts ot the world were devastated. People lost their homes, cities were destroyed and factories were ruined. When the war was over it was impossible for those countries to carry on manufacturing or other normal pursuits. We had none of that in this country. In addition there was a ready market for practically everything that we could manufacture after the war.
Today the situation is changing. Those countries which were devastated during the war have now built up their factories, and their people are back to work. They are producing in competition with our Canadian people. Our trouble seems to be that our economy has been carried on in such a way that we cannot compete with these people who have built up their factories and gone back to work. Today they are taking overseas markets from us which in the past were so necessary to our economy.
So I say that the third part of this amendment moved by the opposition is the most important. It may be that we have been carrying on the wrong type of businesses in this country. I do not know whether all of them should be continued. It may be that we should concentrate mostly on manufacturing the great raw materials which we have within our borders. These are all things that could be studied by a committee.
I have pointed out before that it is not right for us to concentrate most of our industry in the central parts of this country. There should be a policy of decentralization so that people in the maritimes and in western Canada would have an opportunity to get employment without having to leave their homes and go to other parts of the country. It may be that our channels of trade are changing, that instead of moving across the country from the east and west, as the economy of this country was set up, they are moving north and south. We have lost those overseas markets which were so precious to us in the past. We have been concentrating on one market, a market which I am sorry to say could be closed against us at any time at the whim or pleasure of the people with whom we trade. Then there is the matter of tariffs. I am not an authority on tariffs and I do not intend to discuss them at this time.
I was quite impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) the other day when he spoke of taxes and wondered if we were not taxing ourselves, not only out of the foreign market but also out of the domestic markets. Foreign 83276-150
Proposed Committee on Unemployment countries are able to produce much more cheaply than we can here in Canada. The hon. member claimed, and I think rightly, that taxes are so heavy today in this country that the individual cannot buy the goods manufactured in his own country. The taxes paid by the manufacturer are so high that he cannot compete with manufacturers in countries like Japan and Germany and numerous others in other parts of the world.
I think there is a lot in that argument. All these things could and should be studied by the committee which our party has recommended should be set up. We may be told that this is a function which the cabinet should perform. I am not going to discredit the cabinet, nor do I agree with the hon. member for Halifax or the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), that the ministers are as capable as they say they are. I am no hero worshipper, when it comes to this cabinet. I agree that it contains some able men, but I am inclined to agree also with the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) when he says that most of them are just run of the mine. I have sat across from them here for 18 or 19 years. Some of them are indeed able men and the service they have given to this country is incalculable. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway says, the majority of them could be replaced by the backbenchers at any time and from most any place in the house. Mr. Speaker, I rise mainly to challenge the government to take at least one step in connection with this matter right away. When I say "right away" I mean that the government might well hold a cabinet meeting yet today, or certainly before the house meets tomorrow, with a view to bringing in a bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
That has already been suggested by delegations which have waited upon the government, and it has been suggested a number of times during the course of this debate that the time has come for the benefit rates paid under the Unemployment Insurance Act to be increased, and for the length of time for which unemployment insurance benefits can be paid to be extended.
I remind the government that on a former occasion, when the unemployment situation was regarded as serious, even though the number of unemployed was not as great as it is today, action of this kind was taken in a commendably short period of time by the government on the other side of the house.
I refer to the situation in the winter of 194950. Hon. members will recall that at that time the unemployment figures were worse than they had been at any time following the end of world war II. We came down here for the 1950 session of parliament on the 16th of February. In the speech from the throne which was read at the opening of that session on February 16, 1950, as reported at page 2 of Hansard for that date, a bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, to widen the


scope and extend the benefits of unemployment insurance, was forecast. The then minister of labour, the late Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, was away from the house because of illness and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) was the acting minister of labour. I am sure he will recall, no doubt with pride, that it was only eight days from the time of that announcement on February 16, 1950, until the bill amending the Unemployment Insurance Act, and extending its scope, had been given third reading by this house. That third reading was given on the 24th of February, 1950. Incidentally, it did not take very long for the other place to pass the bill. They can pass bills they regard as urgent in record time, as we well know. Indeed, royal assent had been given to that bill on February 28.
Let me summarize that schedule once again. We met on February 16. On that day there was an announcement that something was going to be done about unemployment insurance, and within 12 days the amending bill was law.
In this instance, the situation is far worse. On that occasion the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as acting minister of labour, gave on page 157 of Hansard for February 23, 1950, the number who were looking for employment as 375,600. The comparable figure today, according to the Minister of Labour, is over 500,000. On that occasion that action was taken, as I say, in a total time of 12 days from the day when the house met until the bill amending the Unemployment Insurance Act became law.

speechtext:
I have the greatest of respect for the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is now Acting Prime Minister. It is because we have respect for his capacity to get things done that we continue to make this appeal to the government now under the direction of the Acting Prime Minister, in the hope that he will yet do something about it, as he can, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has just testified.
If I may, I should like to get back to these figures which the Minister of Trade and Commerce says I have referred to every year. May I draw his attention again to the fact that in each of the years between world war II and the outbreak of the war in Korea, the unemployment figures were worse than they were the winter before. The outbreak of the war in Korea checked that rise from winter to winter. But surely it should give the government cause for concern to find that now, when the situation in Korea has cleared up, the very first winter after that war is


over we start off with unemployment figures which are worse than they were in the winter just before the Korean war. Do the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of National Health and Welfare not see the ominous picture that arises from that fact? Unless something is done, it means that the next winter and the winter after that will be even worse and we will be right in the midst of the serious situation to which the government is trying to blind itself.
I know that the ministers over there on the opposite side do not like this kind of talk. They deprecate it in every possible way. They and others in the house as well as people outside the house do not like the use of the word "recession" or the word "depression"; but in my view the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) was perfectly correct last night when he pointed out that this is not another recession or another depression but that we are still in the same economic condition that started in 1929. It has been relieved for a few years by world war II, by the cold war and by the war in Korea, but the basic economic problems facing the Canadian economy are still with us. Until we are prepared to tackle the necessity of producing the things that people need for peaceful living in the same way as the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as minister of munitions and supply, was prepared to tackle the job of producing the necessities of war, we shall continue to have these economic dislocations which mean unemployment for hundreds of thousands of people and economic distress for a great many of our people.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the seriousness of this situation calls for more than the type of interruptions that we get from across the way and for more than speeches from the government side with regard to which set of figures is correct. I submit that it calls for real action along the lines that have been suggested from this side of the house. The one specific point on which I have urged action this week is not the whole solution to the problem by any means, but it would be one step towards relieving economic distress and it would give the country an indication that the government means business. I hope that some action along that line will be taken with the least possible delay. My main purpose in rising, Mr. Speaker, was to remind the government of the speed with which action was taken in 1950 and to call for an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to be presented to this house by the government this week.

Finally, there is the realization among Canadians that we shall not tolerate conditions as in the thirties. Depressions are not acts of God. There are some I know who have a depression psychosis. As I understand it, the Progressive Conservative party would turn over this problem to some committee; but it has always been my impression, with respect, that that party has never faced up to the economic facts of life. Any kind of planning to them is ipso facto bad, undemocratic and worse. They are always sniping at the moderate degree of public ownership in Canadian life, as witness the ill-conceived attempts to fight Trans-Canada Air Lines, the world's best air line, and the C.B.C. which, with all its faults, is developing, as much as anything else in Canada, a truly Canadian culture.

I think the government role is best set out in a speech by the Acting Prime Minister at Dalhousie University in 1948, when he said:
1.	Canada is a free enterprise economy and the initiative for industrial expansion rests with private individuals and firms.
2.	The government will endeavour, through its policies, to create a climate within which private initiative thrives and industrial expansion is encouraged.
3.	The government will take the initiative and do what it can to co-ordinate the efforts of governmental, business and other interested groups in achieving full and effective utilization of industrial expansion in the interests of all citizens in the country.

4.	If industrial expansion and economic development is hampered by the lack of initiative, the government, where the national interest demands, will take appropriate action.
In conclusion may I say that I do not think it matters too much whether the figures used are those supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics or by some other body. Sometimes when I hear speeches which leave the impression that the attitude of the government is indifferent or callous, I think they are most unfair, because every member in the house, regardless of party, is lending his best efforts to solve this problem. And my experience has been that, with a man like the Acting Prime Minister in charge of trade and commerce, the Canadian people will never have to worry, and we shall come through this thing with flying colours.

subtopic: MOTION FOR EXAMINATION BY COMMITTEE ON INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate on unemployment by reason of the fact that this has been a problem in my constituency for several years. In that constituency the present situation is not seasonal. There is a large coal mining industry in the southern part of the constituency of Macleod and, by reason of circumstances, coal miners in that part of the country have been on short time for a number of years. They have been working one or two or, at the most, three days a week. In fact they are experiencing something in the nature of the hardships which were experienced in the hungry thirties. Therefore I wish to say a few words on this subject.
I do believe there is no use simply blaming governments, blaming individuals, or blaming this, that or the other for this condition. When all is said and done, and when we think the problem through to its ultimate conclusion, we will have to agree that basically it is a matter of policy, and we must decide whether the policy is right or wrong.
In order to do this, sometimes we have to review our thinking and make some adjustments in it. For instance, in a good many cases I find that some people presume that the chief purpose of industry is to give jobs to people, to give employment to the nation; and I believe we must adjust our thinking in that regard. The main purpose of industry is not to provide employment. The purpose of the coal mining industry is to produce coal. The purpose of agriculture is to produce the foodstuffs of the nation. The purpose of the factory is to produce goods. The purpose of the textile industry is to produce textiles.
Proposed Committee on Unemployment The purpose of the clothing industry is to produce clothes. The purpose of industry, therefore, is not to provide employment but to produce goods. Therefore it devolves upon the government to see that those goods are distributed, as a basic policy.
Another thing we must discover in our investigations is just how this condition of unemployment developed. How is it that many of our people are now unemployed? What is the reason? Have we come to a point where we have produced an adequate supply of goods for which there is no relative market? Must we reach that conclusion? I believe the Acting Prime Minister, who must be advised of this situation, should be able to tell us whether we have reached a point which, in general terms, might be described as overproduction. We in this corner of the house do not use that expression. Instead of saying that we have reached a point of overproduction, we say we have reached a point of underconsumption.
The Acting Prime Minister should be able to tell us whether a stockpiling of goods is now taking place in Canada, no matter what those goods may be. Is that the situation? I was informed the other day of a certain industry in Canada-I believe the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) referred to the same industry-which had produced to the point where it had a stockpile sufficient to supply the normal market requirements for the next five years, and as a result they had laid off their men. Some of these men had been with them for 18 or 20 years.
But that is the condition in only one industry. The Acting Prime Minister should know whether that is characteristic of industry generally in Canada. If it is, then the problem cannot be solved by putting these men back to work in the same industry, because that industry has reached its peak of production and has difficulty in finding markets. When we talk about markets we must think in terms of whether or not people have money with which to buy, because that is the only way we can have markets. There is no market where people have no money.
I have listened to the speeches made in this debate, many of which have been reasonably good. However, I have found something lacking in many of them. I have listened to a good deal of history and to the recitation of many figures. I have heard a lot of pulse feeling. We have heard diagnoses aplenty; we have heard about symptoms aplenty. But in reality we have not heard very much about an adequate remedy. I have listened to the speeches with a good deal of interest. If any remedies at all have been proposed
2364	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment they have been only temporary, in the end amounting to nothing more or less than palliatives.
If the liver is sluggish-I can see a doctor looking at me-we take a pill. The pill can do the trick for a little while, but after the effects of the pill have worn off the liver is in the same condition as it was before; it is still sluggish. You can keep on giving pills as long as you like, but that will not make a new liver. We must have something more than palliatives.
I should like to make another diagnosis with respect to the speeches that have been made. I am not going to blame the government for everything. We have been suggesting for a good many years that there should be a reduction in taxes. It is a good suggestion to make, but let us be realistic as well. The government must have revenue, and I am not one to rise in my place and say that the government would not reduce taxes if it felt it could. We believe it can be done, but we also believe that under present financial policy the government is unable to do it.
We have heard a good deal about foreign trade and the loss of foreign markets, and that we must regain those foreign markets. Well, it is easy to say that, but when we ask how you are going to regain them, we find that that is another problem. As I look at the government I am quite willing to suggest that they are just as anxious as anyone else to find foreign markets, and if they could find foreign markets they certainly would.
Then we talk of other matters. Am I going to stand here in this house and believe that the government is so heartless that it would not do something about the matter of unemployment if it could? The problem is there. It is all very well to say that a solution must be found, but what solutions have we proposed? That is the big question.
I know that we want to get through by five o'clock, if we can. Whether or not we can is another matter. I was going to refer to a good many of the speeches that have been made and to read from Hansard, but I shall forgo that and say this. There is a solution to this problem. It could be solved in one of three ways. It could be solved by bringing in a state of extreme socialism. That will solve the unemployment problem; it will put everybody to work, if that is what we want.
I say once again that it is not up to industry to provide jobs. That is not the purpose of industry. We have to readjust our thinking when we consider this problem in those terms. Industry is there to provide goods, to do that job. Somebody over here says that


industry is there to make profits. Well, it is all very well to say that. We go a little further than that and diagnose the situation at its roots.
I want to say this to you, Mr. Speaker. After industry has produced all the goods the nation requires, what should our position be? The worker should be able to go home; he should be able to lean back in his easy chair; he should be able to light his pipe and say well, now, we have surely done a good job. We have produced all of this nation's goods, and now the factory is going to close down; now we can rest for a while. He should be able to do that, but can he? No. And why not? Has industry failed to produce the goods? No; they have done a good job. But instead of that we find everyone running around, arguing and fighting and sending delegations, which of course under present policies they have to do, and working up a great frenzy over a problem that should be regarded as an achievement. We should be able to sit back and say we have produced so much; now, look at what we have achieved. My, we are a great country, we are a great people to be able to do that. No, that is not what we do. We fight among ourselves because our achievement has produced a terrible problem.
I go back and I say that if all we want is to solve the unemployment problem and put people to work, we can do that by bringing in a state of extreme socialism where the whole country becomes a machine and each and every individual in it becomes a cog in that machine. We can do it in that way if we want to. We may have a few barbed wire fences around; we may have a few guards there to watch us and see that we work, but that will solve the problem, if that is what we want.
There is a second way in which this problem can be solved, if all you want is to put men to work. The second way is to bring on a war. Well, now, nobody wants to do that; but a war will put every man to work. Believe me, it is a strange thing, and perhaps we should hang our heads in shame, that it takes a war to distribute the goods we produce. Sometimes it distributes them by destruction and death, nevertheless war is the great distributor.
You can have the extreme socialist state, which will put everybody to work; you can have war which will put everybody to work, but there is a third way to solve it, and that is an adjustment of financial policy that will provide enough money in the people's pockets to enable them to enjoy the vast production that has resulted from a good job done well. Yes, if you want to reduce the hours of labour, all well and good. If you want men

Proposed Committee on Unemployment
to work two, three, four or five days a week, all well and good if, as the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) said yesterday, you can provide them with incomes. But if incomes must come from a delinquent financial policy, from a financial system that is not self-liquidating, then we shall see times of booms and depressions, times of war and times of unemployment continually throughout future generations.
The problem can be solved in one of three ways, and I challenge anyone to say there is any other way to solve it, apart from these three. I will use the three. If you wish, first, sovietism, that will solve it, if all you want is employment. Second, slaughter; that will solve it, if that is what you want. Third, believe it or not, is a proper adjustment of financial policy which we in this corner of the house call Social Credit. It can be done.
I am quite aware that the members of the government want to solve this problem. We talk about old age pensions not being high enough. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is in the house. He is a human being; he is a humanitarian. Do you not think that he would like to raise pensions if he could? Certainly he would, but under our present fiscal policy it cannot be done.
The government is bound by a false financial policy which ties its hands. Let us adjust that financial policy. Let us see that our consuming power matched with money will equate our productive power. Then we will not have the problem of unemployment. We may have shorter hours for peaceful pursuits, and as long as we have our income and can consume we will reach the stage where we will have one of the highest orders of civilization known to man.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the various speakers who have dealt with this problem and the more I have listened the more I am convinced that the problem is only beginning. I feel that we are in the first phase of a new age, a mechanical age, and our growing pains will increase still more as we develop into the atomic age. Therefore we are dealing now merely with an emergency condition.
I shall not repeat what has been said already as to the general conditions existing throughout the country, because I feel there is general agreement on the main fact that we have roughly half a million unemployed in Canada. Two speakers at least have argued that work could be made available for these half million people by a change in government policy. I look at it from this point of view. When there are half a million 83276-151
unemployed within the dominion it means that billions of precious man-hours are lost forever, man-hours of valuable labour are gone forever because of the time element. This is not so much a loss to the individual as it is to the nation. True, there is the loss to the individual of his employment and in many cases his self-respect, and his dependents are penalized through his being idle even temporarily.
During the depression I was active in municipal affairs in British Columbia. Immediately after that depression period the provincial and municipal governments of British Columbia pooled their experiences in an effort to provide a scheme whereby the conditions of the thirties could not be repeated, at least in our particular province. The result is that we have a blueprint of self-liquidating projects ready to be implemented, depending upon federal aid or the provision of funds by the federal government at a low rate of interest. With federal aid British Columbia could eliminate its present unemployment situation by starting these proposed schemes. Every scheme is a sound scheme which has been examined by the engineers of the provincial government, and every one would be a tangible asset to the province and the nation as a whole.
Possibly other provinces as well had the same experience and plans were worked out in case of another depression; therefore I shall not deal with that phase of the matter. The federal government could utilize this valuable fleeting asset of human labour. I suggest that if it wanted to it could develop our national assets without hurting anyone, and employ the maximum amount of human labour.
A total of 125,000 men could be used in reforestation and conservation schemes, for which we already have plans in Canada. Another 125,000 could be used to speed up the construction of the trans-Canada highway, which is bogging down badly throughout the dominion. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know that there is much that I can usefully add to what I said on the second reading of this bill. The branch line proposed will be 15 miles in length extending from Havelock, a divisional point on the main line of the Canadian Pacific between Smiths Falls and Toronto, northward to the site of the American Nepheline mine operation at Nephton. At the present time the mine employs some 150 people. It produces a rock product known as nepheline syenite, which is used in the manufacture of glass and pottery. About 70 to 75 per cent of the product is exported to the United States, with most of the remainder being used in Canada, although there are some exports to other countries.
At the present time the product is transported by truck some 24 miles over a road that is part township, part county and part private, to Lakefield, Ontario, there to be shipped by rail. The maintenance of the road has been largely contributed to by the mining company.
Having a railway line come right to the mine will improve the operation for two reasons. Because of its nature, the shipment and transshipment of this product by truck is not satisfactory, as the rock is reduced to a powder-like consistency before being shipped. The other difficulty is that in addition to the maintenance of the road being an expense, shipment by truck over the road is more inconvenient because the road cannot be kept open during all seasons of the year, and

many plants require regular shipments. One week's delay in shipment may be an important matter in their manufacturing process.
The bill before the house is necessary because the Railway Act requires that any branch line of more than six miles in length can only be undertaken after authority is granted by parliament. The bill of course places no burden on the public treasury. The extension of this line will cost $1,500,000 and is being financed partly by the Canadian Pacific Railway, which will meet one-half the expenditure, and the other half will be recovered from the mining company at the rate of 80 cents per ton bonus on the freight handled until the $750,000 is repaid. Even with the payment of that bonus on the first part of these shipments, the operation will be made more economic by reason of the construction of this railway.
It is anticipated, subject to the necessary authority being granted by this parliament and the concurrence of the board of transport commissioners being obtained, that construction will be undertaken immediately and will be completed in this present summer season. Construction will commence as soon as weather permits, and the project should be completed by the fall.
