subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (voluntary revocable check-off).
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving second reading of Bill No. 4 I feel that I am but giving this house the opportunity to approve of a statute the principle of which was endorsed by the last parliament. I am also giving each of the parties in this house an opportunity to support a measure the principle of which has received the support and endorsation of all the major political parties in this country.
That support has been expressed by the opposition groups in this house on a number of occasions, and on several occasions there have been members of the Liberal party who have also voted for the second reading of this bill. I regret to say, however, that as yet the bill itself has not been passed by parliament. Nevertheless I dare to hope that we are getting nearer the day when the voluntary revocable check-off or some form of union security will be written into our national labour code.
May I indicate briefly what this bill proposes. It proposes that a new subsection be

Industrial Relations
written into the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which is our national labour code. When that new subsection has been written into the national labour code it will then be possible for a trade union-provided that trade union has been recognized under the labour code-to request that the employer concerned deduct or check off the trade union dues of those members of the union who in writing express their desire that that be done, whereupon that check-off would be made. In other words, Mr. Speaker, this is what is known as the very minimum of union security.
I for one-and there are other members in the house, I know, who agree with me- would like to see a greater measure of union security written into our labour legislation. Indeed, some of those who appeared before the committee on industrial relations last year indicated that their only complaint about this legislation was that it did not go far enough. I must make it clear also, of course, that there were those who thought it went too far. But as far as the platforms of the four parties in this house are concerned, all have indicated their approval of the principle of union security; and as I say, this bill proposes the very minimum of union security.
May I take a moment to give the history of this bill, at least so far as recent years are concerned. Back in 1948 we had before us the then new national labour code, namely the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. After second reading it was referred to the committee on industrial relations. When it went to that committee it did not have in it any provision for the voluntary revocable check-off or for any other form of check-off or union security. In that committee, however, my good friend the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll)- who likes having reference made to this matter as often as possible; I am sure it does not embarrass him-proposed that the voluntary revocable check-off should be written into the labour code.
That was not an easy thing to achieve in that committee-the lines of division were fairly close-but we succeeded. The committee passed my hon. friend's amendment and it was written into the code in that committee. We dared to hope that that battle had been won; but when that bill came back to the committee of the whole house in June, 1948, another member on the government side who is no longer with us moved as an amendment that the good work of the industrial relations committee be nullified. His amendment was to the effect

that the voluntary revocable check-off provision be struck out of the bill. I regret to say that that Liberal amendment, striking out what the Liberal member for Spadina had moved in the committee, carried in this house and so we lost the day. However, on that occasion there were 35 members of the House of Commons who voted to keep the voluntary revocable check-off in the labour code.
In 1949 a bill was introduced along this line, but it did not reach the point of a vote. In 1950 this bill which is now before the house was presented in my name, and it reached a vote. When the votes were counted it was found that 45 members had voted for it. That was an improvement over 1948. In 1951 the bill was introduced again. I would point out that on each of these occasions the wording has been exactly the same as the wording that was first evolved in the committee on industrial relations back in 1948. In 1951, when the vote was taken, we found we had made still further progress; 67 members voted for it. That group of 67 included not only all members on the opposition side of the house who were present at the time, but 17 members on the Liberal side of the house. When that number of Liberals differ with their party I submit that we are really making headway. It does not often happen in this house.
The matter did not reach a vote in 1952. Talking out was the order of the day that year. In 1953, however, something else happened. After a fair amount of debate on my bill for the voluntary revocable check-off, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) moved an amendment to the motion for second reading. His amendment was the well-known proposal that the bill be not then read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the committee on industrial relations. I expressed the view that I was prepared to accept that amendment at that time. I said I would rather have seen the bill passed, but that I could see the possibility that if we could get the subject matter to a committee we might do an educational job, might make headway, and might eventually get this provision onto our statute books.
We did not get the law passed, but we made some headway. That committee in 1953 considered the matter very thoroughly and made a most interesting report to the house on Tuesday, April 28, 1953. It read as follows:
Your committee has considered the subject matter of Bill No. 2, "an act to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (voluntary revocable check-off) ", and has agreed to report as follows:
Your committee endorses the principle of Bill No. 2-

I think I should repeat that sentence, as the pith of the report is there: "Your committee endorses the principle of Bill No. 2". Incidentally, last year's Bill No. 2 was exactly the same as this year's Bill No. 4, which is now before us. The report goes on to say:
-and recommends that the principle of the said bill, together with the submissions included in the printed minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee on the subject matter of this bill, be considered by the government in its review and proposed revision of the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which the committee is informed is now under study.
As I have indicated, Mr. Speaker, that report was made to the house on April 28, 1953. On May 5, 1953, as recorded at page 4773 of Hansard, the then chairman of the standing committee on industrial relations moved that the report be concurred in, and after a very short debate the motion was passed. In other words, the report of the committee became the report of the house. The position taken by the committee that the principle of last year's Bill No. 2 should be endorsed became the stand of the House of Commons on May 5, 1953.
I recognize, although that stand was taken by the committee and the house, that the report goes on to suggest that the matter might be further studied by the government in the light of the review we were informed was being made of the whole of the labour code. Still I think it should not be lost sight of that the principle of the voluntary revocable check-off itself was clearly endorsed both by the committee and by the house.
Since that is the position with regard to this matter, I hope it will not take much longer until we have this provision written into the labour law of the country. May I point out that the voluntary revocable checkoff or some form of union security is already in a number of provincial labour codes. I know for a fact that it is in the trade union act of Saskatchewan, the Nova Scotia labour code, the British Columbia labour code, and two or three others as well.
Let it also be pointed out that during the years we have been discussing this matter in the House of Commons considerable progress has been made by those workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction in getting the check-off provision. For example, the railway workers, who constitute the largest group of employees coming under federal labour jurisdiction, now have even more than is sought by the bill. They now not only have a check-off in the voluntary revocable terms that the bill suggests, but they have the Rand formula so that the advantages gained by trade unions for workers on the
Industrial Relations
railways are being paid for by all those who enjoy those advantages. However, some of us still feel very strongly that this is a principle which should be written into our labour law at the federal level so that it will give a lead and encourage the same kind of legislation in those labour codes that do not yet have it, and also so that under the law of this country there will be full recognition of the part that labour plays in our economy.
It is somewhat strange to me that it has taken so long to win a law of this kind. After all, the check-off is something that is practised in respect of a great many other types of payment. We know that during the war there were payroll check-offs for victory bonds and that now in peacetime there are payroll check-offs for Canada savings bonds. There are payroll check-offs for income tax, and also for donations to the Red Cross and various other charitable organizations. It does seem strange that when one comes to this matter there should be the employer resistance to it that there is. It has been argued at times that it would involve a bookkeeping task of some proportions, but 1 have not heard any great complaint from the railways over the fact that they now have the check-off as the result of negotiations a year or two ago. As I say, the bill before us would have the effect of recognizing in law what a great many workers already have; it would extend that right to the few who do not have it yet; and it would also serve to recognize in law the important position that labour occupies in this country.
I have deliberately refrained from trying tq be provocative in presenting the case on this occasion, because it does seem to me that the case for this measure is stronger than it ever was. In view of the history I have already recounted, in view of the growing support for this measure across the years, in view of the fact that all parties are in favour of it, in view of the fact that the last parliament endorsed the principle of this bill almost at the end of its term, I hope that this time the measure will not be longer delayed.
I know the answers that have been made from the other side of the house on former occasions. I know what I think of some of the replies that have been made, but I shall not bother to say that now. I hope that on this occasion there will be no excuses, but that the government, which was the government last May when parliament endorsed the principle of the bill, will on this occasion agree that it is time this minimum form of union security, the voluntary revocable check-off of trade union dues, should be written into our national labour law.

Industrial Relations

speakeroldname: Hon. Milion F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is any part of my duty this afternoon, and it is certainly not my intention, to discuss the history of the bill as the sponsor has already done, or to discuss the merits or demerits of the voluntary revocable check-off as described in the bill. Year after year this matter has been brought forward and discussed at some length. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, it was discussed last session, and when the bill came before the house on second reading it was referred on my motion to the standing committee on industrial relations. The committee gave it very careful study and received a great many representations pro and con, and all of that is duly recorded in the minutes of proceedings and evidence of that committee. Perhaps members of the house who were not here last year would like to refer to that report.
On the 28th of April last the committee made its report to the house, and that report has been read this afternoon by the sponsor of the bill. I think the house will agree that the mandatory part of the report is briefly that the principle of last year's bill be considered while the review and proposed revision of the act is under study by the government. As was stated, the report was accepted by the house on Tuesday, May 5, 1953, and the consideration indicated in the report has been going forward. My department has been carrying out what perhaps might be called a long-term but careful study of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. It has been working out a number of proposed amendments.
I should like to say a word right here about the act. It is not an old one. It is one act that has not been subject to very many amendments, and to my mind it is an act with respect to which the greatest austerity should be exercised in introducing amendments. I am confident that the simpler it can be kept the better, as long as it is a suitable instrument to carry out the tasks in hand. The federal labour relations law should never attempt, I think, to be an omnibus act with the pious hope that it will thus end all real or alleged evils associated with any group of organized employers or organizers workers, because the spirit of conciliation on the part of the bargaining parties to a dispute is of more value than all the amendments that can be attached to the act.
Therefore the officials of my department have wanted to take time in which to review these amendments based upon useful years of experience since the end of the second world war. In fact it might well be that we

should take more time in making sure that, on the one hand, all amendments that would be useful are included and, on the other, that all amendments we do include are absolutely essential. In a process such as this I do not think the committee in the department that has been working on this matter should be rushed. Because of this the group of amendments have not yet been completed by my department, and I of course have not yet recommended that group of amendments to the government.
Now, what has the House of Commons said about the matter? The committee recommended to the house last spring that the principle be considered during the review of amendments I have been talking about. The house endorsed that recommendation. We in the Department of Labour are, in our own time, carrying out that recommendation for consideration.
I am not able to say at this time when I shall be able to submit a final list of amendments to the government. I cannot undertake to give the house the exact time when this action can be taken, or to forecast the results thereof. I do not think the matter is of such great urgency that I should take this step at a time when I would like to have further study given to all the proposed amendments, and also at a time when there still exists in the public mind a very strong feeling regarding the check-off concept, due to certain disputes in which the check-off, even though not this kind of check-off, was an important factor under other jurisdictions.
Therefore I hope the sponsor of the bill will not consider it a discourtesy if, after a reasonable discussion, I should ask one of my colleagues to move that the debate be adjourned.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of talking this bill out; but I cannot understand in this day and age, with the experience we have had with the voluntary revocable check-off, why there should be opposition to this type of union security, particularly opposition from the government.
For a start, the government is pretty well committed to the principle in the bill. The government checks off income tax at the source. This is done in respect of the indemnities of members of parliament. The government also has a very excellent recreation association in Ottawa, and we know that the members of that association pay their dues by the check-off, through government payrolls.
This is not something new in this country. The government has adopted the principle.

I would just like to ask the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) how he would collect his income tax, or how many inspectors and auditors and policemen he would have to employ to gather the taxes he gathers today, if it were not for the fact that those taxes are deducted at the source, by government order.
So, you see, when we begin to argue the principle it becomes clear that that principle is very well established, so far as the federal government is concerned. Some members in the house would say, "This is pretty wide; it is pretty sweeping." Well, it is not. The type of check-off that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) advocates in the bill merely covers industry in this country that may be under federal jurisdiction. There are not many of them-the national harbours board, Polymer, Canadian Arsenals-and most of them have it already.
So there is nothing wide or sweeping about it at all. Organizations that are organized provincially come under the provincial codes, and in most provinces they have this type of check-off. Even if it is accepted and is placed in the code, it is not mandatory. It is arrived at generally by agreement. When a union, recognized through due processes prescribed by law, sits down to write an agreement, such agreement is arrived at between employers and employees, and neither the union nor the employer in this type of check-off can compel anyone engaged in the industry or standing as a member of a union to accept this type of check-off. It becomes a matter of individual selection. With the voluntary revocable check-off the individual must place a card signed by himself in the company office, authorizing the employer to make the deductions. Otherwise such deductions are not made.
On the other hand, if during the term of an agreement union officials get out of line, or a union is not functioning as it should, the employee has the right to go to the office and withdraw his card. There is no compulsion in it. When one considers the fact that throughout the country today this type of check-off is in operation, the present request does not seem unreasonable. I know that in my own province we pay for hospitalization in this way. We pay for our doctors in the same way, under a group system. The churches receive their money by the same process.
I do not see that anyone in the house has anything to fear by writing into the national labour code something that will bring a little more democracy into the industries coming under that code. It is pretty
Industrial Relations
nearly time we got around to this type of legislation, not only because the government accepts the principle but because it is implementing that principle in practically every organization coming under its control, with the exception of the national labour code.
Someone has said that he cannot understand resistance by employers. Well, I can understand it. An employer knows it is very difficult for an organization to function unless this type of dues collection is in operation. If it is not operating, then it means that union officials who wish to collect their dues have to travel continuously, thus occupying the major portion of their time. An employer knows that when a union must function through the voluntary collection of dues it is pretty badly hampered, and that is why he resists. He resists because he does not want the efficient functioning of union financial matters in or around his industry. It is a refusal to grant a little more democracy and to make things a little easier for those who are trying to look after the interests of employees. That is why he resists; make no mistake about that.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, and as the Minister of Labour well knows, we have had this kind of check-off in my end of the country for at least 60 years, and it has not caused any great revolution. The unions established it first, and it worked so effectively that other organizations followed suit, even to the federal government in the collection of income tax. In Ontario a learned judge, Mr. Justice Rand, headed a commission which made a thorough study of the whole question and recommended what has come to be known as the Rand formula. That is a little tighter form of union security, because no member is permitted to contract out of the organization during the life of the agreement. All members must pay their dues during that period.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is not even asking for that. He is asking the government to write into the code a principle that is accepted by themselves, one they have in operation, that gives the employee the right to put a card in the office saying that his employer may take his dues and pass them over to the secretary-treasurer of the organization. And, on the other hand, if he does not like what is going on in the union he has the right to withdraw that card and not support the organization financially. In my judgment there is nothing wrong with it. Those who fear it do so because of the propaganda that is put out by the employer who wants no organization of

Industrial Relations
any kind, and who realizes that this is one of the ways of stopping the union from functioning.
I could give the house a lot of instances in this country where this question has caused a great deal of upset and economic upheaval, loss of wages and all the rest of it. Fortunately in most industries in this country today, where the employer is a sensible and moderate man, it is recognized that a well-established union, with proper leadership, is one of the biggest assets of the organization. I am sure that if the management of the mining industry, the automobile industry and the Canadian National Railways were questioned as to the desirability of having a union or otherwise, they would say, "Leave it there. The best advice we can get in most of our operations is received from the union officials, because they have someone there who meets with us and goes back to the men; therefore we get a lot of things done that we would not get done otherwise".
This means of getting the dues of the employees of an organization is one thing that is necessary to give the union the stability it needs to consider problems that affect industry, rather than have the officials chasing around trying to collect dues and occupying their time in that way. I am sure the Minister of Labour realizes that as well as I do. It seems that there are some stop-blocks behind the scenes that will not give him the green light. He has the red light, and has had it for a long time. I hope that at this time the house will say, let us pass this. The trade union movement is part of the structure of this country; it is as much a part of the country as industry itself, because the ultimate objective of the organization and of the people who work in the industry is to bring it to the point where it may accept responsibility for a share of the management of industry and give us a more effective machine to produce more in this country, for our people to enjoy.
I trust at this time, without any further discussion, this bill will pass and another milestone will be passed in the establishment of industrial democracy in the country.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour has made it clear that it is not the intention of the government to permit this bill to go to a vote. He has stated that he will welcome a motion to adjourn the debate, and I am not in much doubt that he will have the opportunity of extending that welcome, and that he was sure of it before he made the suggestion.
One of the things that interest me today is the different procedure being followed by
[Mr. Gillis.l
the Minister of Labour in relation to the measure now before us. Last year when this same measure was under discussion the government moved that its subject matter be referred to the committee on industrial relations. The motion of the minister on that occasion was:
That Bill No. 2 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations.
I suppose it would have seemed peculiarly inappropriate at this particular time to introduce a motion of that nature suggesting that a select committee or a standing committee could obtain useful information, because we have heard so often in the last two weeks that the reference of any subject to a committee would be to divest hon. members of their responsibility. So it would hardly be consistent on this occasion to turn around and say well, we were quite ready to improve our own position but we are not ready to do that in the case of something that affects the general rights of labour in this country. Possibly the Minister of Labour would not admit that, but at least there is strong reason to believe that something of that kind might have suggested that the axe be used instead of the reference.
I must say that I do not believe it is good practice in regard to this or any other measure simply to rise and say we are going to have a motion introduced which will have the effect of ending this debate. The government may feel that that is a proper course, but it is one which does savour of a denial of the ordinary rights of private members to bring a matter of this kind to its conclusion. Since that position has been stated, in putting before this house certain views that I think I should put forward I am not doing so in apprehension that if I occupy the ten minutes at my disposal I shall be avoiding the possibility of a vote. It has been made quite clear that it is not the intention of the government to permit a vote on this measure.

Oh, I see; no vote now. That ties it to the statement of the Minister of Labour when he said: "I do not think that the committee in the department should be rushed." This committee in the department has been working for years, and

when the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) says the time is not now, then we know that it is to be at some distant date in the future when the committee will finally be ready to make some proposals.
Last year, as on earlier occasions, this same plea was made. We were to wait for the appropriate time. Since we are not going to have a vote now, according to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, then the best we can do on this occasion is to avail ourselves of this opportunity to put forward certain views which have a direct bearing on this subject, particularly on the statement of the Minister of Labour that he does not think the committee in the department should be rushed. Just when this committee would not consider that it was being rushed is something that would really be a matter of interest to some of us. We heard these same discussions on this same bill on earlier occasions.
Since this bill has been up before, and since this does afford us an opportunity to present our views, may I repeat the arguments I presented last year, which were presented on earlier occasions and which I hope may receive the support of the government, because this is an important subject.
I must say that we do not need to be told by any hon. member that the trade union movement is now part of the social and economic structure of our country. That is recognized by every person who has the slightest knowledge of the essential requirements of the relationship between management and labour. However, what is not as readily accepted is the fact that the basic requirement of union security is collective bargaining and the assurance that the duly certified bargaining agents in any industry or occupation will be able to carry forward the work that they are set up to undertake under laws which have as their purpose a balanced relationship among workers, management and the public, who have a very direct interest in the end result of that relationship.
Due consideration must also be given to the inevitable and important relationship between governments and their agencies which have so constant an association with labour and management. The field is divided between national and provincial responsibility. That is something which always must be borne in mind.
We have contended on earlier occasions that this act should not be amended piecemeal, that what is greatly required is a review of the whole act and that an opportunity be provided for organized labour, for management and for representatives of the public generally to place their views before
Industrial Relations
some competent body which will in turn be able to make recommendations which can be the basis of legislation.
Do not let any member of this government or any supporter of this government get up at this time and say this is simply another suggestion to pass over the responsibility of parliament to some outside body. After all, it was this same government that appointed the McTague commission more than eleven years ago. That was the last time a comprehensive survey was made in Canada of possible labour legislation. True, there have been references to the standing committee on industrial relations; true, there have been discussions in this house from time to time on individual measures, but those who have had the responsibility for the administration of legislation of this kind-at one time I also shared some measure of responsibility for the administration of labour legislation- know that piecemeal amendments without due regard to the impact of any amendment on other parts of the act can sometimes defeat the very purpose for which the amendments are made.
At the time the McTague commission made its report after very extensive inquiry the government acted under the wide emergency powers then available to it, and which it was prepared to use. It has just as wide emergency powers today and we are very glad it does not use them, for the present at any rate, or not now, to use the words the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration prefers.
At that time they employed the wide powers of the emergency legislation then available to them and introduced what amounted to a labour code. We came nearer to having uniformity of labour legislation at that time than ever before in Canadian history. Some of the provinces adopted the labour code outright as the provincial code, and as a result there were some provinces in which there was uniform labour legislation, which is highly desirable if it can be reached by agreement.
Eleven years have passed, during which time this country has expanded as an industrial producer beyond the expectations of anyone in those days. That expansion has brought new problems; that expansion has brought new pressures on the legislation we now have before us. If it was wise for this same government to appoint a public inquiry of three under the chairmanship of a distinguished jurist of that time, then I submit it is equally wise that the same course be followed today.
It should not be said that this is divesting us of responsibility, nor should it be said

Proposed Committee on Unemployment that a judge, or in this case one who has been a judge, is not a suitable person to head such a commission. Without in any way expecting that the government will accept my suggestion in a case of this kind, I may say that I for one would welcome their decision to appoint the same man as chairman of another commission. I think most members of the unions in Canada approved of the appointment at that time of Mr. Justice McTague, and would approve today the appointment of Mr. McTague as chairman of a commission to conduct an inquiry with similarly wide terms of reference.
Since this government has already demonstrated its belief in that method; since they were able to act so satisfactorily on the recommendations then presented to them, and since they incorporated most of the provisions of the order in council resulting from those recommendations into subsequent legislation which is still on the statute books, I repeat my request that a similar committee be set up because the government is not ready to act now, and I underline the word "now".
Since they are not ready to act now, then will they follow the same course they followed before and appoint a competent body, including someone with a wide knowledge of labour relations, including at least one representative of organized labour and one representative of management? If they were going to appoint a committee of three that would seem to be a well-balanced body. On that basis we might then have recommendations before us which would make it possible for us to have as fine labour legislation as would be available anywhere, and next year we would not be faced once again with the statement that the government is not ready to act now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I tried to point out the serious loss unemployment meant to our economy. Half a million idle men means billions of man-hours of labour lost, especially when the idleness is prolonged. Idleness means billions of dollars to our economy. I outlined briefly the plans drawn up some years ago by the British Columbia government in co-operation with the various municipalities affected, and in view of the fact that these plans could be put into operation if the government would assist them I think the matter should now be considered.
The government, I feel, should perhaps consider giving to the towns and provinces which are prepared to co-operate once again some assistance by means of low interest long-term loans, especially for self-liquidating projects and those things in which the money could be safely invested in the form of mortgage finance, if necessary. During the thirties the government did actually assist the municipalities to tide over a very embarrassing period of unemployment by outright money gifts, financial help, and by making other funds available. I remember when I was on the Kelowna council we received quite a substantial grant from the federal government to assist us in putting numerous men to work on a sewer project.
I always look back to those days and feel that instead of keeping those men on relief- there was no unemployment insurance in those days-we saved the social services money and produced real, valuable assets of a permanent nature which were necessary to the town's development with labour which otherwise would have been lost forever, instead of subsidizing the social services which in turn would permit men to remain idle.
I listened last evening to the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) reiterating the statement that what is physically possible could be financially possible. I agree with him. That statement is quite correct. But I do not agree with his method of printing money to make it possible. To my mind that is straight inflation. I would suggest a logical and proper way of bringing these two factors together and making financially possible what is physically possible, and that is by the government making loans through the Bank of Canada to municipalities for investment in self-liquidating projects where possible. The cost of the operation and the service charge for bookkeeping and other expenses in connection with the issuance of that money at no more than 2 per cent could be borne by the municipalities. I am satisfied it could be done. I am not suggesting even then that this is a permanent solution, but it might

meet the present emergency and grant us time to really meet the problem which arises out of machine age development.
To my mind the day is not far distant when we shall be compelled to adjust our whole economy to meet the challenge of machine-produced abundance, because we know that today it embarrasses us, and will embarrass us to a greater degree when the atom is fully harnessed, to produce commodities that will create such abundance that human labour will become absolutely redundant. The present unemployment problem is simply an advance warning of the trouble to come from that source, and it is for the government to advance policies which will immediately take care of the displaced human labour today.
Some years ago I remember reading in a western paper about a wealthy easterner, I think he lived in Toronto, who had a habit of throwing his money out of hotel windows with a prodigal disregard for his own security. Probably some hon. members will remember the incident. At that time his sanity was questioned, and possibly rightly so; nevertheless that was what happened. I feel the government today is doing just that. We are throwing away billions of precious man-hours of labour which are being wasted and becoming an embarrassment instead of an asset through being channelled into productive work.
I realize that we are living in an age when human labour is becoming more redundant every day. With the advance of science and technology today we are witnessing the need for labour in industry receding accordingly. Private enterprise has no solution for our present problem. It has no solution for the displaced labour at this time except in terms of a hot or cold war, neither of which is acceptable to the Canadian people.
This condition to my mind calls for skilful direction by the government to protect the victims of the modern industrial process. Private enterprise will not do it. It is their failure in this respect that we have been discussing in the last few days. They naturally prefer the machine, where possible, to human labour. The machine operates 24 hours a day, does not strike for better conditions and produces more profits at a quicker pace than human labour. But such a policy will inevitably lead to chaos and distress even for the industrialists themselves.
Long-range planning should therefore be undertaken by a government which should be prepared to study even social credit and socialistic proposals to find a possible solution. Immediately, however, the government should set up a committee, or instruct the Department of Labour in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities, to study
Proposed Committee on Unemployment and produce a program of development which would be of permanent value to the nation. Why fritter away millions in supporting enforced idleness when such labour could be utilized to increase our national wealth? The unemployed are themselves chafing at the bit for work to do, and the government must give the lead.
We in the opposition will gladly co-operate in any way we can to make it possible for the government itself to bring order out of what may possibly become extreme chaos and hardship for our workers here in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take just a few minutes of the time of the house to comment on this subject, and I make no apology for explaining my position in this connection.
I have just listened, as did other hon. members, to the last speaker. I hold no brief for the government, but when I hear someone in this house get up and say private enterprise has no solution to this problem except a hot or cold war, then I am rather surprised. I can understand the socialists saying that private enterprise has no solution, because that is the basis of their philosophy. They and they alone have a solution. But though I have listened to a great many speeches by members of the C.C.F. party, thus far I have not detected their solution. I do not think the government obtains any information of value from that particular section of this house.
The hon. member who has just spoken, at the tail end of his remarks, said we were discussing the failure of private enterprise, and that in this country we preferred machines to human labour. Well, I wonder how far this country, the United States, or any other progressive country would have developed if it had not been for the technological research and the evident skill and ability which private enterprise produced, which is manifest in the economic situation prevailing in this country and in the United States today. We do have machines in this country. We have an automobile industry in Windsor and Oshawa which could compete with any other in the world today except for taxes.
Machines create employment for labour, as the record of history will prove, and no socialist inside this house or out will ever convince me that machines replace human labour. We are told they are chaos and distress machines. I do not think anyone outside that party will agree with that. True enough we all admit-the members on both sides of the house-that we have an unemployment situation. We have yet to find anything in the socialist doctrine that is going to solve that problem.
2376	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
I must say first that over the last several years we have heard the government justifiably boast that they are going to maintain full employment. What is meant by unemployment? Is it half a million people out of work? Or is it seasonal unemployment? I want to be fair, and I think every hon. member in this house wants to be fair. No one can tell me or anyone else in this house that we have not seasonal unemployment. We have other unemployment as well. The other day I think a suggestion was made by one hon. member-I am sorry I have forgotten his name-who said it should be the responsibility of government to devise, maybe through advisory boards, some way by which these seasonal employees could be employed for a longer time. I think the idea is well worth consideration. I have no doubt that the government advisers are considering such ideas with that as an objective.
I want to be quite frank and say here that while I am sympathetic to labour, I do not quite agree with their idea expressed here and there that industry has the responsibility of maintaining full employment by the year or, in other words, paying a yearly wage. That will come in time. It may come sooner than many of us expect, but at the moment I cannot see it, in this changing economy, with the competition facing us today, when industry would naturally be placed at a disadvantage if it should overproduce. Today in this country and in the United States we are in the position where we have overproduced. True enough that is a better position to be in than to be underproducing, whether it be wheat, automobiles or socks.
In the course of this debate we have heard about the unemployment in the textile industry and the farm implement industry.
I was amazed, as I think many people were, the other day when a delegation met some of the members of the cabinet. When this situation was being discussed by the cabinet members and the representatives of labour the Acting Prime Minister told this particular delegation representing those who were out of work in either the farm implement industry or the textile industry that they should go somewhere else to seek employment. I rather think it was one of those statements made on impulse.
Of course what strikes me is this. That is a rather impossible position for those people to face. In the first place, where would they go? In the second place, the town or the city to which they went might also have unemployment. After all is said and done,
I do not think there are many places in the Dominion of Canada today which have not unemployment. If these people were to


migrate from one town to another and were to almost vacate some particular town or small city, there would be a bankrupt municipality.
I think the federal government must accept some responsibility. I am not saying that this philosophy of ignoring the almighty dollar, the value of that dollar, its purchasing power, and the necessity for conserving it, is not worthy of great consideration. I never did like the philosophy of "What's a million?" or "What's three million?" Nor do I subscribe to the theory that building, say, a $6 million national film board building is going to alleviate unemployment, especially when there is some doubt in the minds of many people as to the necessity for that particular building.
With respect to public spending, I am going to say here that I think the federal government should be the first agency in this country to endeavour to alleviate present conditions and get the wheels of industry turning so the dinner-bucket man can take home his weekly pay cheque. In that connection I am going to say this, and it is something which has been supported recently by press editorials. We in this country have been enjoying an export trade as well as taking care of our own requirements and competing against foreign imports into our country to replace those things we manufacture. I think what we must keep in mind in this country is that we have excessive taxes including the sales tax, the excise tax and other hidden taxes which go into the costs of the product which we hope to export in competition with foreign products, and with which we hope to supply our domestic market in spite of foreign competition.
I am rather afraid that many of us in this country will have to agree that these excessive taxes are pricing us out of the export market, and are also pricing us out of the local market as against foreign competitors. We in this country have become an industrial nation during and since the war. Prior to that time, of course, we were an agricultural country. In order to maintain a healthy economy I think we must enjoy a fair export market. Otherwise these men who depend on weekly pay cheques are going to find those pay cheques smaller, and that later on they will cease to come.
I would say that the responsibility today is on the federal government to take the initiative in this country, as was done on the other side of the border some few weeks ago by curtailing expenses as far as they possibly could. I think they appreciate the situation their country is in. In all fairness to any

government that is in power I am going to say that what happens in the country to the south of us, whether it is good times or bad times, is bound to be reflected in this country. We just cannot get away from that nearness and the fact that they produce much the same things as we do, especially those products that we export and that they export to this country.
When we see people out of jobs it reminds me of something I heard on the radio a few weeks ago-and probably many other hon. members heard it-when they were talking about "recession" and "depression" which we heard a great deal about in the thirties. A recession is when the other fellow is out of a job, and a depression is when you are out of a job. I think that is quite true. You do not realize how hard up you are, what position you are in or what you have to face until the ordinary man with the dinner bucket finds himself on the short end of a pay envelope.
We are faced with that situation. We must acknowledge that fact. I will say that governments must realize that they are in somewhat the same position as that of housewives. There are some things they cannot afford; and if they cannot afford them, they cannot spend themselves into a recovery. I believe in public spending-I am one of those in this house who do believe in it, and I think I have many associated with me- but I believe there is a long-term view as well as a short-term view of this particular situation.
The government has taken the stand that this is a temporary situation. That may be right. By the end of another month we may reach the turning point. I hope we do. In any event it would appear that the budget is not going to be brought down until sometime in April, and that will give the government an opportunity to homestead for another six weeks before doing anything about the matter.
I think my interpretation of public spending should be acceptable to many people, and I hope to members of the cabinet. I make no apology for saying that the construction of public buildings, the filling of the backlog of orders so to speak, in case we ever run into a recession, which we discussed some years ago when municipalities were urged to put forward their ideas as to what should be done, would afford but temporary relief to the unemployed. I agree with an hon. member from Nova Scotia who spoke a few nights ago, who said that in so many of these projects in this country and elsewhere the
Proposed Committee on Unemployment amount of labour involved is so small compared with the total capital investment as to cast doubt on the wisdom of certain types of public spending even in times like the present.
I do not think we can spend ourselves out of a recession. My idea of public spending at a time like this would be along the lines of that held by private industries who see a future expanding market and want to enlarge, and who would invest $1 million, $2 million or $5 million, as the case may be, to expand their particular industries in order to take care of business two, four, five, ten or twenty-five years from now.
With the technological advances that have taken place today I think even some of our most modern industries will not be modern four or five years from now. The point I have in mind with respect to the idea I have been trying to convey is simply this. To my mind there are projects in this country that we could undertake which would be beneficial in this respect, namely if the government would do as industry does and spend $2 million, $4 million, $5 million, $50 million or even $100 million it would help to alleviate present conditions and at the same time would have long-range benefits.
For instance, there is the Passamaquoddy power project in the maritimes, which would be a federal matter and would mean a great deal to that particular part of the country. I could go on and recite others such as a power and conservation development on the Fraser river at the other end of Canada, as a result of which acreage under production would be increased in the course of time and the yield would be many times what it is today. I would call such projects developments of productive capacity which would appeal to the imagination of every Canadian. I cannot see, for instance, why the Saskatchewan river project could not be undertaken at the present time as a federal matter. Here we have a power project that in the years to come will benefit thousands, hundreds of thousands and possibly even millions of Canadian people. It may take 10, 15 or 25 years to achieve the benefits, but let us look ahead.
We are going to get over the hump. Let there be no mistake about it. Canadians will remain Canadians and will face any difficulty. All we want is good leadership, and we need not worry about what is going to happen tomorrow or the next day. Let us take a long-range view. These are the types of projects which the government should undertake because they are self-liquidating.
2378	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment
With respect to hidden taxes, I think the time has come when the government must realize that if we are going to have a sound economy, keep our industries growing and reopen the ones that have been closed, we must remove some of these nuisance taxes, the sales tax, the excise tax and other excessive hidden taxes, because we are pricing ourselves out of the market. I say quite frankly, and I will say so to any labour organization in Canada, that labour as well as management has a responsibility to cooperate. If they are true Canadians then they must accept the responsibility that is theirs. The necessity for endeavour on the part of every Canadian was never more apparent since the thirties than it is today. No one party, no one government, no one province, no one municipality can solve the problem. It requires the co-operation of everybody.
I say it is the responsibility of the federal government to give leadership. So far as hidden taxes are concerned, we had an illustration a few years ago of the result of excessive taxes on cigarettes. Since I first entered the house these taxes have been increased, and the government were told that their revenue would be decreased. I am not going to discuss the necessity for the reduction of taxes on cigarettes, but the point I make is simply that when taxes were increased on this particular product the revenue decreased. We urged that the taxes be reduced. I am sure the government will admit in all fairness, because the records are there to prove what I say, that they are very pleased with what has happened during the last year as a result of the reduction of these taxes. If the taxes had not been reduced we would not have had the same consumption, and as a result would not have had the revenue.
Because we have these excessive taxes we are bound to encourage smuggling. We are actually subsidizing foreign manufacturers by our excessive taxes. That applies without any question to cigarettes and to many other products. In this country we have a great acreage of tobacco and should have much more. By reducing taxes we increased revenue. I say the same principle should apply to the taxes on so many things we buy. I repeat, and I do not mind doing so because if an idea is worth uttering it is worth repeating, that I think the public realize today as never before that hidden taxes, the sales tax and so on, are so oppressive that the workingman is losing his job. Why? I think he realizes today as never before that he is being taxed out of his job by the policies of the present government.

I could give several quotations but I do not intend to. However, here is one that substantiates what I said about the construction industry. Representatives of the Canadian construction association presented a brief to members of the cabinet the other day. I have here an article from the Ottawa Journal of February 22 dealing with that meeting, from which I intend to quote only a paragraph, as follows:
It said construction is desirable in times of general decline in business activity, but this year Canada will have a high volume of construction anyway. "It is very doubtful", the brief said, "that a substantial increase in the public works program would affect the present seasonal unemployment . .	. or help the textile, marine, agricultural
implement and other industries currently beset with serious unemployment problems".
That is in line with what I said a few moments ago. While we are bound to have a construction program this year of no mean amount, as I endeavoured to emphasize a few moments ago, in my conception public spending during this period on a works program of buildings and so on would provide only temporary relief. I would much prefer to see that coupled with a long-range program involving projects such as I have put forward. I refer to the Fraser valley, the Passamaquoddy, the South Saskatchewan and many other projects in which the federal government could participate.
I want to say something else related to this particular subject with which I do not think anybody will disagree. We have in this country the greatest potential tourist industry on the continent per capita, and we are not getting our fair share. While the tourist industry affects every section of our economy, and everyone in business, we seem to disregard it. I would say that this is one industry in Canada from which everyone benefits, when our American friends come here and when in return we export good will. I think the government should take the lead in this matter, but it never has. It cannot make the claim that it has done anything to promote the tourist industry. Instead of obtaining something more than $300 million from the tourist industry, I say we should be obtaining a billion dollars, and I said that ten years ago. The tourist industry has actually decreased in dollar value in the last few years.
I believe that under an aggressive program initiated by the government we could bring in that amount of money. This would mean a great deal to people in Canada from coast to coast, not only those operating tourist services and resorts, but people in all sorts of businesses.

Proposed Committee on Unemployment
I hope the government will consider at this time the plight in which the municipalities find themselves. My own conviction is that many of those municipalities are going to find themselves under a very severe strain because of this unemployment, the necessity of supplying relief, and also because of the high taxation policy of the government. For many years now they have not received their fair share of tax revenues. I am inclined to think that if this matter goes much further the government will have to appreciate the position in which the municipalities are finding themselves. I am sure no hon. member would like to see his own municipality suffer and not be able to meet its obligations, or to take care of relief measures, or fulfil those other requirements which, as municipalities, they must fulfil.
I would express the hope that before too long this government will realize that governments at lower levels have responsibilities. This applies to provinces as well as to municipalities, and affects all the people. In my opinion it is about time these lower levels of government secured some kind of agreement under which they would be placed in a respectable and responsible position, so they could meet their obligations and not feel called upon to be under any obligation to any other government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I make no apology for speaking on the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). In my opinion the very serious unemployment problem now under debate demands the utmost attention from those in responsible positions. As a representative of the people of Canada I wish to express my opinion as to what should be done, and to make some comments concerning the whole situation.
It has been established, and I believe accepted on the government side of the house, that the figure of about 525,000 unemployed is accurate. This represents about 7 per cent of the total labour force in Canada. So no one can underestimate the serious situation facing our country unless something can be done to rectify the situation and to put those people back to work under some program.
I listened with keen interest to the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) who attempted to castigate the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Jones) for his references to the capitalist system. I refer to it as a capitalist system, not a so-called free enterprise system, because certainly there is nothing free and there is nothing
very enterprising about the system under which we operate. It is a capitalist system; and I quite agree with the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary and other members of the C.C.F. who have expressed little or no faith in capitalism as a means of obtaining security in peacetime for our Canadian people. Looking back as far as I can recall, over a period of years we have gone the full cycle of employment, recession, nonemployment and then back to full employment, when our people had jobs and a decent standard of living.
When he reflects upon what he has said I believe the hon. member for Lambton West will realize the truth of what I am saying, and that he was mistaken when he applauded the capitalist system which has done nothing but bring unrest, unemployment and insecurity to the world. Today when we have such great opportunities through technological advances we should be able to use our natural resources in order to get jobs for everyone, so that all people may have a decent standard of living, and security.
I was interested before the dinner recess to listen to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) who tried, as he said, to indicate three methods by which the situation could be corrected. One of those methods he said would be a very clear socialist policy. I do not know what he meant by that; he did not go to any length to indicate his meaning. In any case I want to take issue with him, and to correct his statement that industry does not operate to give employment. Let me tell the hon. member that if in Canada we have investors and if we have people in control of multimillion dollar companies, then it is their responsibility to give employment to our people. They have a responsibility to keep the factories open to give our people jobs.
It is true that the giving of jobs is not the primary endeavour of industry; nor is it as he suggested, the production of goods. The production of goods in industry, I say, is only secondary to the profit motive. The production of goods is only incidental to the making of profits. It is clear that on those occasions when they cannot sell their goods and make profits, neither goods are produced nor people employed. And that is pretty well what we are finding in the Canadian economy today.
Therefore I suggest that we must give consideration to ways and means by which our people can share equitably in the economy of this country. Today we have in Canada, even under the system now operating, a condition under which we are
2380	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment using about $2 billion of our Canadian gross product for war preparedness, or defence production. Our total gross product in Canada in 1953 amounted to about $24 billion. If we take that figure of $24 billion and take also the population of Canada which, roughly, can be placed at 15 million people, and allow a certain amount-perhaps a third-for capital investment, we still have a figure under which every family of four would enjoy an income of $6,400. When we make allowance for depreciation in capital investment to the extent of one-third of our national product, and make an equitable division, we still have a family income of $4,500. We know for certain that it is not possible to divide it equally. Perhaps we would not be justified in dividing it equally, but it does show that in Canada we are producing a gross national product which could take care of any hardship in the country.
That is not being done. I hold in my hand a sessional paper dated January 29, which I received some time ago. This sessional paper gives the number of people making income tax returns for 1951-52 in certain salary ranges. It shows that 452,427 people earned less than $500 a year; 443,140 earned between $500 and $999; 601,655 earned between $1,000 and $1,499; 690,792 earned between $1,500 and $1,999; 750,889 earned between 2,000 and $2,499 and 476,134 earned between $2,500 and $2,999. This sessional paper shows that today our people are not enjoying what might be called a decent income.
This government has a definite responsibility to see to it that our people are protected in their jobs. We can pick up almost any paper today and see the large profits that are being made by our large industries, particularly those in a monopoly position or with such control over the market that they can demand from the consumer practically any price for the commodities they have to sell. From that we can see why our Canadian products are being priced out of the picture in so far as international trade is concerned.
I know some hon. members will say that labour itself has so increased the cost of Canadian products that our goods are no longer able to compete in the foreign market. That is not true. For proof of this statement all we have to do is to look at the farm implement industry. That is one of the industries that sent delegates to Ottawa to interview the cabinet and ask that something be done. We find that despite the increases in wages from 1946 the profits of


the machinery companies per dollar of product produced have increased to a far greater extent than have wages.
Therefore we find ourselves in a situation similar to that of the 1930's. Sufficient money is not going back into the pockets of the people who produce the goods to buy back that which they produce. Great technological strides have been made in the production of commodities, and the Canadian people should be able to buy those products for use in their homes to enable them to maintain a better standard of living. Our government should take the responsibility of seeing to it that more money goes back into the pockets of the people to buy back what is produced. If that is not done, exactly the same thing will happen as happened in the 1930's, when we had unemployed men riding the box cars throughout the country. Our factories were shut down, and that may happen again.
I do not think it is to the credit of any system that we have to have war or threats of war in order to keep our people employed, or to give them a high standard of living. The cruel irony of it, Mr. Speaker, is that our people have never had a higher standard of living or fuller employment than when we were at war, when almost half of our national product and our resources of manpower were engaged in war production. Surely it does not take too much common sense to be able to make the point that when we are coming back to a peacetime position we should be able to organize our economy and use technological improvements to increase the standard of living of our people.
Here is the position in which we find ourselves, in spite of the fact that certain people are willing to start new enterprises. The figures I am about to give the house do not in themselves indicate that it is of necessity a good thing, but in the last quarter of 1953 there was an increase in the total number of established commercial enterprises. In the third quarter of 1953 the number increased from 2,554 enterprises to 3,131. In the month of September there was an acceleration of commercial failure. The total number of commercial enterprises operating at the end of September was in excess of those operating at the end of July, but that is not the point. The point is that in dollars the total volume of money invested in those enterprises had declined.
I think hon. members will be interested in the figures I am about to give. They indicate the grand total amount of money in such commercial enterprises. We find that until

1929, up to the time we had the crash, we were enjoying a period of pretty good prosperity. Then the crash come. From then until 1939 there were a very large number of commercial failures. The situation began to get better; the amount of money invested in such commercial enterprises began to go up until the war came, when there was great investment in commercial enterprises. Then we find in 1953, after the period of the cold war, an increase in commercial failures.
I have tried to outline some of the reasons why the government should take immediate action in this held. I would suggest that some of the measures the government has taken in the last two or three years are not going to be effective to stave off a calamity for any long period unless something else is done.
I recall that in 1951 the government took off practically all credit controls, and we found that instalment and credit buying increased very rapidly. We found that by September 30, 1953, an appalling situation existed in connection with outstanding instalment debt. At that time there was $225 outstanding in instalment debt for every Canadian. This has almost tripled in the last 18 months. The total instalment debt, charge accounts and personal loans up to date stand at $500 per family. The debt situation of the Canadian family is increasing to an alarming extent. I think the government should find ways and means of dealing with that sort of situation.
There are some things the government could do in order to restore the purchasing power of the Canadian people and put many of our people back to work. First, I would suggest that farm purchasing power be restored. Someone will hasten to his feet to say that in 1953 we had an all-time record farm income, but when we take the farm income for 1953 and the figures of farm purchasing power in connection with the things the farmer has to buy, we find that the farmer is in a very bad position in that relationship.
I ask the government to consider putting adequate floor prices under farm commodities and taking over immediately, through the wheat board, 500 million bushels of wheat. I feel that the Canadian farmer, along with every other Canadian, is willing to do his share in seeing to it that the hungry people of the world are fed. I think that would be a tremendous gesture on the part of a democratic world to help alleviate hunger as well as win support for democracy. In addition, I submit that the government should increase the old age pensions. The present payments
Proposed Committee on Unemployment to our older citizens in the form of old age pensions are a disgrace. This would give our older people a more decent income so they could enjoy some of the amenities of life and buy some of the goods now on the shelves that Canadians have produced, and thereby help the situation. I suggest to the government that it abolish the 10 per cent sales tax which today has the effect of increasing the cost of farm machinery and reducing the effective demand of the farmer for such machinery, as well as increasing the prices of commodities to the general consumer.
In addition I think the government should undertake a very comprehensive and imaginative program in respect to public works projects. I recall that when I was here from 1945 to 1949 we as members of parliament understood that the government had a shelf of public projects which it was prepared to utilize in case unemployment ever struck the Canadian scene. If that is true then I think it is high time they pulled out of the dark any secrets they may have in this regard. The Canadian people are asking that something be done.
Then, I feel that the government should take steps to reduce the interest rate so farmers and others may be able to obtain credit at lower rates. It is nothing short of usury the interest which people have to pay, whether on farm improvement loans or when they get a loan from the bank. Certainly those people who through force of circumstance have to go to these finance corporation people in order to get short-term credit at 24 per cent interest are paying rates which are a disgrace to the country.
I just want to close by saying that this is a serious problem, but a solution can be found if the government has the will to do it. Just as we won the war so we can win the peace. The veterans and all our people generally are placing the responsibility at this time on the people right here in this government, namely the Liberal government. The delegation representing the unemployed people in the farm implement industry who came here were not at all satisfied with the answer they got from the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe). A statement appeared in the press to the effect that the Acting Prime Minister had told them that they must find other jobs. The headline read:
Must find other jobs, Howe bluntly advises farm implement men.
I want to say to the right hon. minister and to the government that these workers are victims of circumstances beyond their control. All they can do is come to their elected representatives and ask them to do
2382	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment something. Under our complex society most of the jobs are governed by industrial employment, and the wheels of the factories must turn. If it is a matter of public investment, then it has to come from the people in charge of the public treasury, namely the dominion government. On these two counts I would ask the government to do something.
It is not sufficient to tell these labour people to leave their former places of employment, to leave their homes and families and go to hunt other jobs. These people are not Dick Whittingtons who can put their little bags on their backs and strike out to find work. If they think the streets of Ottawa are paved with gold because of the money talk there has been around the house these last few weeks, they will find otherwise. These people want work, and they want it now.
These 500,000 unemployed represent potential wealth. After all, wealth is only that which is produced by the working people applied to the natural resources. If we consider the daily output of each of these people when fully employed to be worth $10 to the nation, it would mean that these 500,000 men could in 200 days produce $1,000 million of wealth a year. If we consider that in terms of $10,000 homes, we find that 100,000 homes could be built for people who need them.
So I ask the government to consider this matter seriously. The people want an answer. The motion of the hon. member for Cape Breton South indicates that we want action now.

I was intrigued by the wishful thinking on the part of the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) when he 

indicated that he expected that the industrialists of this country might use the benevolent despotism which it was the custom of the early industrialists to use. I think we have reached a situation where we have a corporate industry which has very little human sympathy. Indeed we cannot expect that human sympathy will be exercised.
I can remember what has happened even within as short a period as my own lifetime. I am thinking of a factory owner in my native Northern Ireland who produced linen. When unemployment came along he used his assets and the profits which he had plowed back into business in order to keep what he called "my people" in employment, and he did that until he had used up all the resources he had in his possession. I would suggest that now he would be considered as a man not quite right in his mind.
I was intrigued by something said by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), and particularly by his three S's, sovietism, slaughter and social credit. It was a neat piece of alliteration, and I suppose my hon. friend would not like me to suggest that these things are three of a kind. I shall not do so. But I would like to point out to my hon. friend that if his solution of handing out purchasing power is correct, then there are only two ways in which to do it. You can take this purchasing power and say to a man, "Now, here is what you need. When you need more come back and we will give you some more." That is the first method. The second method would be simply to hand out this scrip or money indiscriminately-

I would like to ask my hon. friend who is to take charge of this public purse, because whoever has charge of it will have a regimenting and dictatorial power greater than any power any democratic socialist ever dreamed of, and one to which I am sure no one here has ever aspired.
On the question of unemployment, we in the prairie country are perhaps more fortunate than people in industrial areas. We have not very many industries, and such industries as we do have are largely connected with the construction business. It is admitted, though, that when the temperature is 30 or 40 degrees below zero there must be some seasonal unemployment, and I would point out that that seasonal unemployment is serious to the people who are concerned. I would like to see some way of overcoming the difficulty.
I have a good deal of sympathy with the government in their difficulties in dealing with

this situation, because they have come around to what my hon. friend from Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) has described as the difficult stage in an inevitable cycle, which during my lifetime has cropped up on several occasions. We have always been faced with the three conditions of depression, followed by war, followed by depression and then back again, and we have reached a definite place in that cycle which has occurred for the third time in my lifetime.
Many people here have said, and I expect there are many others who agree with them, that war seems to be the thing which does away with unemployment and depression. I am very interested in young people and in the education of young people, as some of my friends know, and I think one of the most serious aspects of this situation is that these young people are faced with this alternative, whether to choose war or choose depression. The danger is that they may make the decision in favour of war. As a matter of fact, I noticed in a United States magazine the other day that a survey had been conducted among some colleges in that country and the young people there had been asked, "What has war done for you?" Nearly all of them, I was horrified to observe, agreed that "War is the thing to which I owe my chance for an education."
That, Mr. Speaker, is a terrible condition of affairs, and I am worried lest the young people may come to believe that the only way they can avoid a depression, or the only way in which they can get a job or an education, is by means of war, or lest they conclude that that is the lesser of the two evils. As a matter of fact one of these young men said, "Yes, a few of us kids may get killed, but there will be lots of us left and it will be a lot better for those who are left." That is not a dream. That is an actual fact, and it is something we have to be prepared to face.
I have already mentioned the unemployment situation in my own city. There is considerable unemployment there, though I believe it is mostly seasonal. The condition, of course, is worse in those cities where we have industries which are making consumer goods, and here again we run into that same cycle at a time when the shelves have become full. That is true in the textile and agricultural machinery industries; most of these industries which are producing consumer goods are now, in the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, piling up a backlog, so much so that he was forced to say to a labour
Proposed Committee on Unemployment delegation, in my hearing, that that was the sort of trouble they had to expect in times of peace-
