When the shelves are full then those in modern Canadian industry-and we could not call them benevolent despots-cannot afford to keep men in employment, and they shut the mills down so that unless we have a Korea or war or some other crisis there is a long period of attrition during which these shelves are being emptied of their goods, and the men are out of work. They have fulfilled their function for the time being and filled the shelves, and they can go on unemployment relief. It takes money to purchase goods, and the result is that in peacetime it takes a lengthy period before conditions are brought about again in which there is a demand for those goods and the men can be put back to work.
That condition has been aggravated by the process of mechanization, and I would suggest in that regard that the situation is liable to become worse in time rather than better. It is an old story. We have had it since the time of the industrial revolution, when men burned the looms because they believed they were depriving them of employment. I suggest the time has come when we must accept these problems and arrange to meet this process of mechanization. It is the government's responsibility-I am glad it is not mine-to take these bumps out of business so we can have an economy which will work. The problem, then, seems to be to get the goods off the shelf.
There is one other word I wish to add, namely that in the meantime I believe some of the recommendations we have heard here are going to be of some help. The problem concerns that fabulous or fabled shelf of public works of which we heard in 1945 or 1946. If some of these suggested solutions were put into operation they would, I believe, provide some alleviation, but I do think the main problem has never been answered. So I would be pleased if I could hear from some of my friends on the government side who would be prepared to answer this simple question. What is the government's solution?

Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) a short time ago, I was pleased to note that I found myself in complete agreement with one rather weighty observation he made. That observation was to the effect that it was the responsibility of government to give leadership. Prior to that I had been thinking that possibly he and I might be able to get together in a mutual admiration society in reverse in respect of the contributions which our political groups were making to this debate.
As far as I have been able to understand the remarks coming from that section of the house, I can briefly sum up their contribution by suggesting that they are advocating that we set up a committee to call before it certain people who will give us the statistics on unemployment which have already been given to us by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). Had they suggested that the government and the Minister of Labour should consider revising their methods of gathering and tabulating figures so they might possibly be more accurate and more complete in detail than they are at the present time, there might have been some point to their argument.
In the course of this debate some of my colleagues have discussed some of the broader aspects of unemployment as a symptom of an economic disease in our society. I shall therefore attempt to confine myself for a short time to some of the aspects of this matter within the terms of reference which have been set by the government itself. I recall that earlier in this debate the Acting Prime Minister made note of the fact that plans have been laid for an investment of something over $5 billion in Canada in the coming year. He suggested that this investment would be a means of eliminating, in large part, the present unemployment that everyone agrees exists, even though we may have varying ideas as to its proportions. In passing I should like to point out that while $5 billion sounds like quite a lot of money to most of us, a quick calculation shows that if it were all spent in wages it would provide $1,000 to each of the 500,000 unemployed that some people have suggested there are in this country today. However, as I say, I mention that matter simply in passing.
I would agree that some of that $5 billion about which the Acting Prime Minister was


talking is going to be spent in that great nation-building tradition of this country which was set when the Canadian parliament quite some time ago launched the building of the first national transcontinental railway in this country. I would suggest that such things as the oil pipe line and the St. Lawrence seaway are in that nation-building tradition. I wish the Acting Prime Minister had elaborated a little bit more on just how and by whom this $5 billion was going to be spent. I have a feeling that the largest part of it will be spent by a relatively few large corporations. I should like to give one example of what actually can happen when these large corporations are investing capital in new plant and equipment.
I call to mind an investment which was made last year by one of the largest and, in my opinion on the basis of its record, one of the most efficiently and intelligently managed corporations operating within the province of British Columbia. They made additional capital investment in their plywood industry. It is perfectly true that for a period during the summer months there was a great humming of activity, and that jobs were provided for a large number of men in the construction trade. As a matter of fact they were being called upon to work a good deal of overtime in order that the project might be completed and brought into production. Of course quite a large number of people flocked in to secure jobs in the production line in that enlarged plant.
The actual situation, as it developed, was that before that new plant had been run in to the point of its maximum output, that company found itself in the position where it was laying off some of these recently-hired employees, some of the people who had come there in good faith expecting to find continuous employment. Not only were the workers who had been engaged in the construction of that plant out of work; people who had the expectation of normally steady employment in the production line were also out of work.
I use that example to show that large capital investment in itself is not necessarily any guarantee of continuous and stable employment. I would further suggest that when you find large investments being made by a few perhaps competing corporations simply to improve their own position and secure for themselves a larger share of an existing market, the result of that investment is simply going to be instability and insecurity of employment.
In my opinion the real solution to this problem, as has been suggested by some of the other hon. members who have spoken,

Proposed Committee on Unemployment
lies in the adoption of investment, trade and industrial management policies which this government have indicated they are not prepared to adopt. Of course the fact that these people are sitting in the seats of government is, as far as I am concerned, an indication that the majority of the Canadian people have not as yet seen the necessity for adopting those policies either. But there is one policy and one principle which I submit this government has accepted as being valid and proper. I refer to the insurance principle.
We have a national unemployment insurance plan. I would say there is no question that the majority of the members of this house have accepted that plan as basically a good idea, and also that the majority of the Canadian people have accepted it as a good idea. The only criticism that arises in respect of it is as to its inadequacies, as many people see them.
What does this plan of unemployment insurance that we have today do? I think that subject was fairly well outlined by the Minister of Labour when he suggested that it provided some protection against what he called frictional unemployment, and against seasonal unemployment. That is perfectly true. While many of us might point out that the amounts payable are in many respects inadequate, we would not deny that it does offer at least some measure of protection to those who become unemployed and who have been contributors to the fund. But I do not think anyone in the house would argue that it is not correct to say there are wide gaps in the coverage provided by the present plan.
There is the question of having to have the required number of contribution days. In the case of the lay-off that took place last summer, to which I referred a few minutes ago, I know that a large percentage of the people caught in that lay-off were recent immigrants to this country who did not have the required number of contribution days under the plan in order to qualify for unemployment insurance. Consequently people whom we had welcomed to this country, people to whom we had opened our doors, in many cases found themselves suffering severe hardship, with no prospect of gainful employment throughout the winter and no prospect of being able to draw unemployment insurance benefits.
I remember quite well an incident that occurred on an airplane trip I made last summer, and I think this is a rather good illustration of what happens to some people who follow the advice given by the Acting Prime Minister and go other places to look for jobs. I was travelling on the plane
over a rather rugged section of the west coast of Vancouver island. My seatmate turned to me and said, "See those poor chaps sitting over there on the other side of the plane." I said, "Yes". To me they were obviously people who had come from one of the eastern sections of Canada. He said, "Those four men are going to land in Vancouver within the next half hour, and they are going to land there broke."
These young chaps had followed the dictum of the Acting Prime Minister, and in line with his and another such dictum has gone west, as far west in this country as they could go. They had landed in a logging camp, and had been given jobs. About a week later they were laid off because of the fire season. They had paid their fare there and their fare out. They had paid for their logging boots and other necessary heavy clothing. But they were going to land in Vancouver broke through no fault of their own but rather as the result of their initiative in going to that rather remote part of our country. I doubt very much if those men would receive any help under our present unemployment insurance plan.
If the insurance principle is valid, and if the government is prepared to admit that it is, then I suggest that the time has come to bring the unemployment insurance plan in line with what is the generally accepted concept of insurance coverage. If I take out a life insurance policy this evening and through some misfortune I am not living tomorrow morning, I expect that my wife will be covered by the benefits provided by that plan. I suggest to the Minister of Labour and the government that the time has come when there should be no question in the house and in the minds of the people of Canada about the acceptance of the principle that unemployment insurance should provide such coverage that if a man goes to work and makes only one contribution, he will have become insured and will be able to enjoy the protection of the plan if through no fault of his own he no longer has a job. That is the kind of change in our present unemployment insurance scheme which, while not offering a solution to the unemployment problem, undoubtedly would alleviate much of the distress existing in the country today concerning which the amendment proposed by this group suggests that there should be some action.
I respect the concern of the Minister of Labour, who is responsible for the administration of the unemployment insurance fund, that the fund should be maintained in a sound position. I think there can be no
2386	HOUSE OF
Proposed Committee on Unemployment quarrel with that, but I suggest that the amount of between $900 million and $1 billion now in the fund represents a sufficient cushion to enable the government to make the necessary adjustments and establish a basis which will give greater coverage under an actuarially sound plan. If the predictions of the Acting Prime Minister prove to be correct and the various things he has outlined do produce relatively full employment during the coming year, I suggest that is all the more reason why such a change should be made in the unemployment insurance plan at the present time. If his predictions do not prove to be correct, then I would suggest that again is all the more reason the government should make haste to make adjustments which will provide the proper kind of protection for all people who become unemployed. People who are not covered and people whose benefits are running out need, more than any others, to be brought under the umbrella of a comprehensive insurance plan.
However, even if that kind of change is made in our unemployment insurance scheme it still will not cover much of the unemployment existing in the country today. The plan will still leave protection against unemployment and the problems arising therefrom unprovided in many respects. It will cover seasonal unemployment, frictional unemployment, any unemployment of a relatively temporary nature, but will still leave uncovered all those who become unemployed on a more permanent basis through changes in market demands.
According to statements made from the government benches, the textile and farm implement industries are good examples of industries faced with such a situation. As the Acting Prime Minister said, he sees no prospect of all the people who were employed in the farm implement industry being reemployed. The plan will still leave uncovered people who become unemployed through various technological advances. In this respect I suggest that the situation of the coal miners of the country is a good illustration of what is happening. It still leaves uncovered those who become unemployed through depletion of our natural resources, such as our mines and forests.
I remember a number of years ago a friend telling me that he had walked out of a certain community in British Columbia leaving twelve houses and a steam laundry. He was at that time a man in his middle years, and had to walk away and leave what represented half a lifetime of industry and thrift on his part. Following that, in his middle years he was engaged as a labourer, with no possibility of


ever again accumulating the sort of protection for his old age which he had thought he was building up. And if he had been living today-he is not-I am quite sure he would be having to subsist on $40 or $50 a month from an old age pension.
All-wise captains of private industry move in and establish industries. People come flocking to them in good faith, expecting to be able to fill jobs. They build homes and establish communities. In their financial calculations these industries make provision for the depreciation of plant and the depletion of resources, all of which are deductible for income tax purposes. In many cases these plants during a period of adverse market conditions can be placed on a caretaker basis for an indefinite period of time, or can be operated on a restricted scale.
I know that in the section of the country in which I live, for the last number of years industrial plants have been operating to capacity on a two or three shift basis. Overnight that picture could change to a point where half that community would be cut off, simply by a decision that it was necessary to reduce the operation to a single shift basis.
In all of this no provision is made for the protection of the workingman's only capital asset, which is his labour. I would suggest that that is a capital asset which cannot be put in mothballs, like a navy waiting for another war. When a man's labour ceases to bring in returns, everything depending upon it must go by the board. People have simply to walk away from a lifetime of work, leaving everything to rot or in the hands of financial wolves who are only too ready to move in when circumstances of that kind develop.
I suggest it is time to do something more than review our unemployment insurance plan. It is time for the government, in line with its acceptance of the validity of the insurance principle, to launch a new insurance plan, one which I would call re-establishment insurance. This plan would cover those people the Acting Prime Minister has advised to go elsewhere to seek work. It would insure them against the loss of their homes, and against having to walk away and simply leave behind everything they have accumulated over a period of years. It would be a plan which would cover retraining these people in another industry, so they might continue to enjoy a level of income comparable with that which they had in the industry from which they had been squeezed out. It would also cover those workers who have reached advanced years. While they might not yet have reached the point where they were eligible for old

age pensions or benefits of that kind, it would cover their enforced retirement so they could continue living on a decent scale.
A short time ago the government had no hesitation in introducing a provision in a bill to insure mortgages. I suggest there are circumstances in which things more important than mortgages should be insured. To my mind it would be more important to provide insurance which would act as a guarantee of stability for the individual worker, so that he would not have to sacrifice all that he had spent years working for.
If the government agrees with the insurance principle, then I say here is a field into which it could enter at the present time. There is very little quarrel in Canada over the fact that plans which in effect were a form of insurance were made for the re-establishment of veterans returning from the last war. Generally speaking that procedure was acceptable to the people of Canada. It was considered sound and valid, and all across the country we have seen beneficial results flowing from it.
I see no reason why some expert study should not make it possible to work out a plan on an actuarially sound basis which would provide a similar kind of insurance for people who have been displaced in industry because of technological change, changes in trade policies of the government, activities of competitive industries in other countries, or any of those other things which are certainly far beyond the control of the individual working man. Without trying to go into detail as to how it could be worked out actuarially, I suggest such a plan could be financed at least in part by a depletion allowance taken from industries when they are created, such sums to be paid into a public reserve fund instead of a private fund, in the manner in which funds for the depreciation of plant and the depletion of natural resources are allocated.
What I have been saying is in line with the one point upon which I was pleased to note the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the Acting Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance seemed to be in complete agreement, and that was that unemployment was important even to one unemployed person, in so far as that individual himself was concerned. In the light of statements made by various ministers in which they have set forth in general terms the manner in which they are willing to act, I suggest the matters I have brought to the attention of the house are such as to merit serious consideration by the government at this time.
If nothing else is accomplished in this debate, I would hope that it would result in
